topics.name: Description
topics.description: Description is a form of writing that presents the qualities, features, appearance or characteristics of a person, place, object, event or situation.
content: Meaning and purpose of descriptive writing
Use of precise and vivid language
Use of adjectives and descriptive expressions
Understanding details and relationships in descriptive passages
objectives: Identify the main subject or idea being described
Understand words and expressions in context
Infer information from a descriptive passage
Identify the writer’s attitude or purpose
Distinguish relevant details from less important information

lesson.title: Description
lesson.introduction: A descriptive passage gives the reader a clear picture of a person, place, object, event or situation. In JAMB Use of English, descriptive passages may be followed by questions testing details, vocabulary, inference and the writer’s purpose.

sections.title: What Is Description?
sections.content: Description presents the characteristics or qualities of something so that the reader can form a clear understanding of it. It may describe appearance, size, shape, colour, condition, location or other features.

sections.title: Descriptive Language
sections.content: Descriptive writing often uses precise nouns, adjectives and other expressions to communicate specific details. The meaning of a word should always be interpreted according to the context in which it appears.

sections.title: Sensory Details
sections.content: A passage may describe what can be seen, heard, touched, smelled or tasted. These details help communicate the qualities of the subject.

sections.title: Reading for Details
sections.content: When answering questions about a descriptive passage, locate the relevant part of the passage and distinguish information that is directly stated from information that must be inferred.

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: An inference is a conclusion reached from information provided by the passage. The answer must be supported by evidence in the passage rather than by outside assumptions.

sections.title: Writer’s Purpose and Attitude
sections.content: The writer may describe something to inform, explain, criticize, praise or create a particular impression. Word choice and the overall tone can provide clues about the writer’s attitude.

keyPoints: Description focuses on the qualities or characteristics of a subject.
Pay attention to precise descriptive words and expressions.
Use the passage as the main evidence for your answer.
Interpret vocabulary according to context.
Do not confuse inference with information that is directly stated.
The writer’s word choice can reveal attitude and purpose.

examples.question: A passage gives detailed information about the appearance, clothing and behaviour of a person. What type of passage is this?
examples.solution: It is descriptive because it focuses on the characteristics and qualities of the person.

examples.question: If a word has several possible meanings, how should its meaning be determined in a comprehension passage?
examples.solution: Its meaning should be determined from the context in which it is used.

examples.question: What should you do when a comprehension question asks for an inference?
examples.solution: Use information in the passage to reach a reasonable conclusion. Do not rely on information that is not supported by the passage.

topics.name: Narration
topics.description: Narration is a form of writing that presents a sequence of events or tells a story. A narrative passage may involve characters, events, setting, time and a particular point of view.
objectives: Identify important characters and their roles
Identify the setting of a passage
Infer information from a narrative passage
Understand vocabulary and expressions in context
Identify the writer’s purpose and attitude

lesson.title: Narration
lesson.introduction: A narrative passage tells a story or presents a sequence of events. JAMB questions on narrative passages may test your understanding of events, characters, setting, vocabulary, inference and the writer’s purpose.

sections.title: What Is Narration?
sections.content: Narration presents events in a sequence. The events may be real or fictional and are usually connected through characters, actions, time and place.

sections.title: Sequence of Events
sections.content: Pay attention to the order in which events occur. Words such as before, after, later, eventually and meanwhile can help establish the sequence.

sections.title: Characters
sections.content: Characters are the people or beings involved in a narrative. Consider what they say, do and experience because these details can reveal their roles and motivations.

sections.title: Setting
sections.content: Setting refers to the time and place in which events occur. Details about location, period and circumstances can help explain the actions in a passage.

sections.title: Cause and Effect
sections.content: Narrative events are often connected by causes and consequences. Identify why an event happened and what happened as a result.

sections.title: Point of View
sections.content: A narrative may be presented from different points of view. Pronouns and the narrator’s access to information can help identify the perspective from which the story is told.

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: Narrative passages often require conclusions to be drawn from events and character behaviour. Any inference should be supported by evidence in the passage.

keyPoints: Narration presents a sequence of events.
Pay attention to the order of events.
Identify important characters and their roles.
Setting includes time and place.
Look for relationships between causes and consequences.
Use context to understand unfamiliar words.
Base inferences on evidence from the passage.
The narrator’s point of view can affect how events are presented.

examples.question: A passage tells how a boy left home, travelled to another town and eventually returned. What type of passage is it?
examples.solution: It is a narrative passage because it presents a sequence of events.

examples.question: A character loses his job and later struggles to pay his bills. What relationship exists between the two events?
examples.solution: Losing the job is the cause, while the difficulty paying bills is a consequence.

examples.question: When answering a question about why a character acted in a particular way, what should you use?
examples.solution: Use evidence from the passage, including the character’s actions, words and circumstances.

topics.name: Exposition
topics.description: Exposition is a form of writing that explains, informs or presents ideas clearly. Expository passages often explain a process, concept, situation or subject using facts and logical organization.
objectives: Identify the main idea of an expository passage
Understand explanations of processes and concepts
Distinguish facts from explanations and opinions
Understand vocabulary and expressions in context
Draw conclusions supported by the passage

lesson.title: Exposition
lesson.introduction: An expository passage is mainly written to explain or inform. Unlike narration, which focuses on events, exposition focuses on ideas, information, processes and explanations.

sections.title: What Is Exposition?
sections.content: Exposition explains a subject clearly and systematically. It may provide information about a concept, describe how something works or explain why something happens.

sections.title: Main Idea
sections.content: The main idea is the central point the writer wants the reader to understand. Supporting details provide evidence, explanations or examples related to that central idea.

sections.title: Cause and Effect
sections.content: An expository passage may explain why something happens and what results from it. Look for relationships between causes and their effects.

sections.title: Comparison and Contrast
sections.content: Some passages explain similarities and differences between two or more subjects. Words such as similarly, unlike, however and whereas may signal comparison or contrast.

sections.title: Processes
sections.content: An expository passage may explain how something is done or how something works. Pay attention to the order of steps and the relationship between them.

sections.title: Facts and Opinions
sections.content: Facts can be supported or verified, while opinions express beliefs, judgments or viewpoints. Understanding this distinction can help with comprehension questions.

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: Some questions require conclusions that are not directly stated. The conclusion must follow logically from information provided in the passage.

keyPoints: Exposition mainly explains or informs.
Identify the main idea before answering detailed questions.
Supporting details develop the main idea.
Look for cause-and-effect relationships.
Watch for comparison and contrast signals.
Follow the sequence when a process is being explained.
Distinguish facts from opinions.
Base conclusions on evidence in the passage.

examples.question: A passage explains how rainfall is formed and describes each stage of the process. What type of passage is it?
examples.solution: It is expository because it explains a process.

examples.question: A passage discusses two methods of farming and explains how they are similar and different. What method of organization is being used?
examples.solution: The passage uses comparison and contrast.

examples.question: What is the main idea of a passage?
examples.solution: It is the central point or message that the writer develops throughout the passage.

topics.name: Argumentation and Persuasion
topics.description: Argumentation presents reasons and evidence to support a position, while persuasion aims to influence the reader’s beliefs, opinions or actions.
objectives: Identify the writer’s main claim or position
Recognize reasons used to support a claim
Determine the writer’s attitude and purpose
Evaluate whether an argument is adequately supported

lesson.title: Argumentation and Persuasion
lesson.introduction: Argumentative and persuasive passages attempt to establish a position or influence the reader. Understanding the writer’s claim, reasons, evidence and conclusion is essential when answering comprehension questions.

sections.title: Argumentation
sections.content: Argumentation presents a position or claim and supports it with reasons and evidence. The purpose is usually to convince the reader that the position is reasonable or valid.

sections.title: Persuasion
sections.content: Persuasion seeks to influence what readers think, believe or do. A persuasive passage may use facts, examples, emotional language, questions and strong assertions.

sections.title: Main Claim
sections.content: The main claim is the central position the writer wants the reader to accept. Supporting points are used to develop and defend that position.

sections.title: Reasons and Evidence
sections.content: Reasons explain why the writer supports a particular position. Evidence may include facts, statistics, examples, observations or other information used to support those reasons.

sections.title: Counterarguments
sections.content: A counterargument presents an opposing view. A writer may acknowledge or respond to an opposing position in order to strengthen the main argument.

sections.title: Facts and Opinions
sections.content: Facts can be supported by evidence, while opinions express beliefs or judgments. A strong argument may combine factual evidence with reasoning.

sections.title: Persuasive Language
sections.content: Persuasive writing may use carefully chosen words to create emphasis, urgency or emotional response. The meaning and effect of such expressions should be considered in context.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The conclusion brings the argument to an end and may restate the main position or show what the writer wants the reader to accept or do.

keyPoints: An argument normally contains a claim supported by reasons and evidence.
Persuasion attempts to influence the reader.
Identify the writer’s main position.
Separate reasons from evidence.
Distinguish facts from opinions.
Look for opposing views and responses to them.
Pay attention to persuasive language and tone.
The conclusion often reinforces the writer’s position.

examples.question: A writer argues that students should read daily and supports the claim with research findings and examples. What makes the passage argumentative?
examples.solution: The writer presents a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence.

examples.question: A passage repeatedly uses strong language to encourage people to protect the environment. What is the likely purpose?
examples.solution: The writer is attempting to persuade or influence the readers’ attitudes or actions.

examples.question: Why is evidence important in an argument?
examples.solution: Evidence supports the writer’s claims and gives the reader a basis for accepting the argument.

topics.name: Comprehension Skills
topics.description: Comprehension skills involve understanding explicit and implied information in a passage, identifying main ideas and supporting details, interpreting vocabulary in context, making inferences and recognizing the writer’s purpose, tone and attitude.
objectives: Identify the main idea of a passage
Understand information directly stated in a passage
Determine the meaning of words in context
Identify what pronouns and other reference words refer to
Identify the writer’s tone and attitude

lesson.title: Comprehension Skills
lesson.introduction: Comprehension means understanding what a passage communicates. JAMB comprehension questions can test information stated directly as well as ideas that must be inferred from the passage.

sections.title: Main Idea
sections.content: The main idea is the central point of a passage or paragraph. Supporting details explain, illustrate or develop the main idea.

sections.title: Explicit Information
sections.content: Explicit information is directly stated in the passage. When a question asks for a fact stated in the passage, find the relevant information rather than relying on memory or outside knowledge.

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: An inference is a conclusion reached from information provided by the passage. It may not be stated word-for-word, but it must be supported by evidence in the text.

sections.title: Vocabulary in Context
sections.content: A word can have different meanings in different situations. To determine its meaning in a passage, examine the surrounding words, sentences and overall context.

sections.title: Reference
sections.content: Questions may ask what a pronoun or other reference expression refers to. Read the surrounding sentences carefully and identify the noun or idea being referred to.

sections.title: Relationships Between Ideas
sections.content: Ideas in a passage may be connected through cause and effect, comparison, contrast, sequence, example or explanation. Signal words can help identify these relationships.

sections.title: Tone and Attitude
sections.content: Tone describes the feeling or manner expressed by the writer, while attitude refers to the writer’s position or feeling toward the subject. Word choice provides clues.

sections.title: Writer’s Purpose
sections.content: The writer may aim to inform, explain, describe, entertain, criticize, persuade or express an opinion. Consider the passage as a whole when identifying its purpose.

sections.title: Answering Comprehension Questions
sections.content: Read the passage carefully, identify the exact part relevant to the question, compare the options with the passage and avoid choosing an answer merely because it sounds reasonable outside the passage.

keyPoints: Read the passage before answering its questions.
The main idea is the central point.
Supporting details develop the main idea.
Explicit information is directly stated.
Inference must be supported by evidence.
Use context to determine vocabulary meaning.
Check what reference words point to.
Look for relationships between ideas.
Tone and attitude are revealed through word choice.
Choose answers based on the passage, not outside assumptions.

examples.question: A passage states that heavy rainfall caused flooding in a town. What can be inferred?
examples.solution: The rainfall contributed to the flooding. The inference is supported directly by the stated cause-and-effect relationship.

examples.question: In a passage, the word "remarkable" is used to describe an unusually successful student. What should you consider when determining its meaning?
examples.solution: Consider the surrounding context. Here, "remarkable" means unusually impressive or noteworthy.

examples.question: A writer explains the causes of a problem and proposes solutions. What is the likely purpose?
examples.solution: The writer is mainly explaining the problem and may also be attempting to persuade readers to consider the proposed solutions.

topics.name: Summary
topics.description: Summary involves identifying and expressing the main points of a passage briefly and accurately without unnecessary details or distortion.
content: Distinguishing main points from supporting details
objectives: Explain the purpose of a summary
Identify the main points of a passage
Distinguish important ideas from supporting details
Paraphrase information without changing its meaning
Avoid introducing personal opinions or information not contained in the passage

lesson.title: Summary
lesson.introduction: A summary presents the essential points of a passage in a shorter form. A good summary preserves the important ideas while leaving out unnecessary examples, repetition and minor details.

sections.title: What Is a Summary?
sections.content: A summary is a shortened version of a passage that contains its essential ideas. It should communicate the original meaning accurately and clearly.

sections.title: Identifying Main Points
sections.content: Read each paragraph carefully and determine what idea the writer is mainly communicating. Important points should be distinguished from examples and explanations that merely support them.

sections.title: Relevant Information
sections.content: Only information necessary to answer the summary question should be included. Minor details, repeated ideas and unnecessary illustrations should normally be left out.

sections.title: Paraphrasing
sections.content: Paraphrasing expresses an idea using different words while preserving its original meaning. It is useful when constructing concise summary answers.

sections.title: Concise Expression
sections.content: A good summary uses clear and economical language. Avoid unnecessary words, repetition and long explanations.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.content: A summary must not change the writer’s meaning. Do not add personal opinions, assumptions or information that is not supported by the original passage.

sections.title: Combining Ideas
sections.content: When several parts of a passage express closely related ideas, they can often be combined into one concise statement.

keyPoints: A summary contains the essential ideas of a passage.
Separate main points from supporting details.
Remove repetition and unnecessary examples.
Use concise language.
Paraphrase without changing the original meaning.
Do not add personal opinions.
Do not introduce information that is not in the passage.
Keep the answer focused on what the question asks.

examples.question: A passage says that regular reading improves vocabulary, develops concentration and increases general knowledge. What would make a good summary?
examples.solution: Regular reading improves vocabulary, concentration and general knowledge.

examples.question: Why should unnecessary examples be removed from a summary?
examples.solution: Because a summary should focus on the essential ideas rather than minor supporting details.

examples.question: What happens if a summary introduces an opinion that was not expressed by the writer?
examples.solution: The summary becomes inaccurate because it introduces information that is not part of the original passage.

topics.name: The Lekki Headmaster
topics.description: The Lekki Headmaster by Kabir Alabi Garba is the prescribed literary text included in the JAMB Use of English syllabus. Preparation should focus on understanding the story, characters, themes, events, language, setting and the relationships between ideas.
content: Lessons and ideas from the text
objectives: Identify the author and title of the prescribed text
Recall important events in the story
Identify major characters and their roles
Explain how characters develop through events
Identify causes and consequences of important events
Make logical inferences from events in the text

lesson.title: The Lekki Headmaster
lesson.introduction: The Lekki Headmaster is included in the JAMB Use of English syllabus. Questions can test understanding of the text, characters, events, ideas, language, mood, attitude and implied meaning.

sections.title: How to Study the Novel
sections.content: Read the prescribed text carefully and keep track of major events, characters, settings, conflicts and important developments. Avoid relying only on isolated summaries because examination questions may test relationships between different parts of the story.

sections.title: Plot
sections.content: Know the major events in their correct sequence. Pay attention to what causes each important event and what consequences follow from it.

sections.title: Characters
sections.content: For each important character, study their role, personality, actions, relationships and development. Pay particular attention to how characters respond to major events.

sections.title: Themes
sections.content: Identify the major ideas developed by the text. Be able to support each theme with relevant events or character experiences from the novel.

sections.title: Setting
sections.content: Study the important locations and circumstances in which events occur. Consider how the setting influences characters and events.

sections.title: Conflict
sections.content: Identify important conflicts between characters, individuals and circumstances, or opposing ideas. Understand the causes and consequences of each major conflict.

sections.title: Language and Expressions
sections.content: Pay attention to important words, phrases, idiomatic expressions and figurative language used in the text. Their meanings should be understood according to their context.

sections.title: Inference and Interpretation
sections.content: JAMB may ask what can reasonably be concluded from an event, character action or statement. Base every inference on evidence from the text.

sections.title: Mood and Attitude
sections.content: Study the emotional atmosphere created in important scenes and the attitudes expressed by characters or the narrator. Word choice and events can provide clues.

keyPoints: The prescribed text is The Lekki Headmaster by Kabir Alabi Garba.
Know the sequence of major events.
Know the roles and characteristics of important characters.
Study relationships between characters.
Understand the major themes and conflicts.
Know how important events affect later events.
Study important expressions in context.
Be prepared for inference and interpretation questions.
Use evidence from the text when answering questions.

examples.question: What areas should a student study when preparing for questions on the prescribed novel?
examples.solution: Study the plot, characters, relationships, setting, themes, conflicts, important events, language, mood, attitude and implied meanings.

examples.question: If a question asks what can be inferred from a character’s action, what should you do?
examples.solution: Examine the character’s action and the surrounding events, then select the conclusion that is supported by the text.

examples.question: Why is it important to know the sequence of events?
examples.solution: Events may be connected through causes and consequences, and questions can test how one event leads to another.

topics.name: Reading Comprehension
topics.description: Reading comprehension involves understanding, interpreting and evaluating information presented in a passage.
objectives: Identify the main idea of a passage
Interpret words and expressions in context

lesson.title: Reading Comprehension
lesson.introduction: Reading comprehension tests your ability to understand information in a passage and answer questions based strictly on what the passage communicates.

sections.title: Main Idea
sections.content: The main idea is the central point the passage communicates. It may be stated directly or inferred from the overall content.

sections.title: Supporting Details
sections.content: Supporting details explain, illustrate or provide evidence for the main idea. Questions may ask you to identify specific information from the passage.

sections.title: Inference
sections.content: An inference is a conclusion reached from information provided by the passage. It must be supported by the text rather than being based only on personal opinion.

sections.title: Writer’s Purpose
sections.content: The writer may aim to inform, explain, persuade, describe, entertain, criticize or achieve another communicative purpose.

sections.title: Tone and Attitude
sections.content: Tone refers to the writer’s attitude toward the subject or people discussed. Clues in word choice and overall presentation help reveal the tone.

sections.title: Words in Context
sections.content: A word may have different meanings in different contexts. Use the surrounding sentences and ideas to determine the meaning intended in the passage.

sections.title: Fact and Opinion
sections.content: A fact can be supported or verified, while an opinion expresses a belief, judgment or viewpoint. Read carefully to distinguish the two.

sections.title: Answering Questions
sections.content: Base your answers on the passage. Avoid choosing an option simply because it is generally true or personally convincing if the passage does not support it.

keyPoints: Read the passage carefully before answering.
Identify the main idea and supporting details.
Base inferences on evidence from the passage.
Use context to determine word meanings.
Pay attention to the writer’s purpose and tone.
Choose answers supported by the passage.

examples.question: What should you identify first when trying to understand the overall meaning of a passage?
examples.solution: The main idea or central point of the passage.

examples.question: What should an inference be based on?
examples.solution: Evidence and information provided by the passage.

examples.question: If a question asks for the meaning of a word as used in a passage, what should you consider?
examples.solution: The context in which the word appears.

topics.name: Summary Writing
topics.description: Summary writing involves identifying the essential ideas in a passage and expressing them briefly and accurately without unnecessary details.
objectives: Identify the main points of a passage
Separate important ideas from supporting details
Preserve the meaning of the original passage

lesson.title: Summary Writing
lesson.introduction: A good summary presents the important ideas of a passage in a shorter form. It should preserve the original meaning while leaving out unnecessary examples, repetition and minor details.

sections.title: Identify the Main Points
sections.content: Read the passage carefully and identify the ideas that directly answer the question or communicate the central information.

sections.title: Remove Unnecessary Details
sections.content: Examples, repetitions, illustrations and minor supporting details should normally be left out unless they are essential to the required answer.

sections.title: Paraphrasing
sections.content: Express the required ideas in your own words while preserving their original meaning. Avoid changing the meaning simply to make the sentence shorter.

sections.title: Conciseness
sections.content: A summary should be brief and direct. Avoid unnecessary introductions, explanations and repeated ideas.

sections.title: Accuracy
sections.content: The summary must remain faithful to the passage. Do not introduce personal opinions or information that is not supported by the text.

sections.title: Grammar
sections.content: Use correct grammar, sentence structure and vocabulary when combining the important ideas into a concise response.

keyPoints: Identify only the important ideas.
Remove unnecessary examples and repetition.
Use your own words where appropriate.
Keep the original meaning.
Do not add personal opinions.
Make the summary concise and grammatically correct.

examples.question: What is the main purpose of a summary?
examples.solution: To present the essential ideas of a passage briefly and accurately.

examples.question: Should every example in a passage be included in a summary?
examples.solution: No. Examples should normally be omitted unless they contain an essential idea required by the question.

examples.question: Can you add your own opinion to a summary?
examples.solution: No. A summary should remain faithful to the information and meaning of the original passage.

topics.name: Comprehension Skills and Question Types
topics.description: JAMB comprehension questions test the ability to understand explicit information, infer unstated ideas, interpret vocabulary and expressions, identify the writer’s purpose and recognize the organization of ideas.
objectives: Answer questions based on information explicitly stated in a passage
Make logical inferences from a passage
Interpret words and expressions according to context
Identify what pronouns and other expressions refer to
Identify main ideas and supporting details
Determine the writer’s purpose and attitude
Draw conclusions supported by the passage

lesson.title: Comprehension Skills and Question Types
lesson.introduction: Comprehension questions may ask about information directly stated in a passage or require you to draw a conclusion from clues provided by the writer.

sections.title: Literal Questions
sections.content: Literal questions ask for information that is directly stated in the passage. Find the relevant part of the passage and make sure the option agrees with what is actually written.

sections.title: Inferential Questions
sections.content: Inferential questions require you to combine information from the passage and reach a reasonable conclusion. The answer must be supported by the text.

sections.title: Vocabulary in Context
sections.content: A word may have several meanings. When a question asks for the meaning of a word as used in the passage, select the meaning that fits the surrounding context.

sections.title: Reference Questions
sections.content: Questions may ask what a pronoun or expression refers to. Trace the reference back through the passage and select the noun or idea that makes grammatical and logical sense.

sections.title: Main Idea and Details
sections.content: Main-idea questions test your understanding of the central message, while detail questions focus on specific information supporting that message.

sections.title: Purpose, Tone and Attitude
sections.content: Consider why the writer produced the passage and how the writer feels about the subject. Word choice and the overall presentation provide clues.

sections.title: Implied Meaning
sections.content: An implied meaning is not stated directly but can be understood from the information and language used by the writer.

sections.title: Eliminating Wrong Options
sections.content: Remove options that contradict the passage, contain information not supported by it, or answer a different question. Then compare the remaining choices carefully.

keyPoints: Literal questions are answered directly from the passage.
Inference questions require conclusions supported by the text.
Vocabulary must be interpreted according to context.
Reference questions require careful tracking of pronouns and expressions.
Main ideas describe the central message.
Tone and purpose can often be identified from word choice.
Never choose an answer merely because it is generally true.

examples.question: If a question asks what a word means "as used in the passage", what should you do?
examples.solution: Use the surrounding context to determine the meaning intended by the writer.

examples.question: Can an inference be based entirely on your personal experience?
examples.solution: No. It must be supported by information contained in the passage.

examples.question: What is the best way to eliminate a comprehension option?
examples.solution: Reject it if it contradicts the passage, is unsupported, or does not answer the question asked.

topics.name: Cloze Test
topics.description: A cloze test requires you to complete gaps in a passage by selecting words that fit the grammar, meaning and context of the passage.
objectives: Use context to complete missing words
Identify grammatical clues around a gap
Choose vocabulary that fits the meaning
Apply logical reasoning to cloze passages

lesson.title: Cloze Test
lesson.introduction: A cloze test removes selected words from a passage and asks you to restore them. The correct answer must fit both the immediate sentence and the overall passage.

sections.title: Read the Whole Passage
sections.content: Read beyond the gap before selecting an answer. Later information may provide clues about the missing word.

sections.title: Grammar Clues
sections.content: Look at the words surrounding the gap. They can reveal whether a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition or another word class is required.

sections.title: Meaning and Context
sections.content: The selected word must make sense within the sentence and the wider passage.

sections.title: Collocation
sections.content: Some words naturally occur together. Recognizing common combinations can help identify the correct option.

sections.title: Prepositions and Conjunctions
sections.content: Pay attention to relationships between ideas. Words such as although, because, however, in, on and at can change the grammatical and logical relationship within a sentence.

sections.title: Verb Forms
sections.content: Use the surrounding subject, tense and context to determine the correct verb form.

sections.title: Elimination
sections.content: Remove options that do not fit grammatically or logically, then compare the remaining possibilities against the entire passage.

keyPoints: Read the passage as a whole.
Use both grammar and meaning.
Check the word class required by the sentence.
Look for collocations and fixed expressions.
Pay attention to tense and concord.
Use logical relationships between sentences.
Do not choose an option based only on the words immediately before the gap.

examples.question: The students were tired ___ they continued studying. (but/because/so)
examples.solution: But. The sentence expresses a contrast between being tired and continuing to study.

examples.question: She is good ___ mathematics. (at/in/on)
examples.solution: At. The correct collocation is "good at".

examples.question: The boy ___ his work yesterday. (complete/completed/completing)
examples.solution: Completed. "Yesterday" indicates a completed past action.

topics.name: Critical Reading and Writer’s Techniques
topics.description: Critical reading involves examining how a writer presents ideas, uses language and organizes information to achieve a particular purpose.
objectives: Recognize the writer’s tone and attitude
Understand how word choice affects meaning

lesson.title: Critical Reading and Writer’s Techniques
lesson.introduction: A passage is not only a collection of facts. The writer chooses particular words, examples and structures to communicate ideas and influence how the reader understands the subject.

sections.title: Writer’s Purpose
sections.content: Determine what the writer is trying to achieve. The purpose may include informing, explaining, persuading, criticizing, describing or entertaining.

sections.title: Tone and Attitude
sections.content: Tone describes the manner in which the writer presents ideas. It may be serious, humorous, critical, sympathetic, enthusiastic, doubtful or another appropriate attitude.

sections.title: Point of View
sections.content: Point of view refers to the perspective from which the writer presents the information. Pay attention to pronouns, statements and the position taken by the writer.

sections.title: Word Choice
sections.content: The words selected by a writer can reveal attitude and influence meaning. Strong or emotionally loaded words may indicate approval, criticism or another attitude.

sections.title: Argument and Evidence
sections.content: An argument presents a position or claim. Evidence such as facts, examples and explanations may be used to support that position.

sections.title: Fact and Opinion
sections.content: Facts are statements that can be supported or verified, while opinions express judgments, beliefs or viewpoints.

sections.title: Relationships Between Ideas
sections.content: Writers may organize ideas through cause and effect, comparison and contrast, problem and solution, sequence or other logical relationships.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The conclusion brings together the writer’s main argument or message. It may be stated directly or inferred from the final part of the passage.

keyPoints: Identify why the writer wrote the passage.
Pay attention to tone and attitude.
Look at word choice for clues about the writer’s position.
Distinguish claims from supporting evidence.
Separate facts from opinions.
Recognize relationships between ideas.
Base conclusions on evidence from the passage.

examples.question: A writer repeatedly uses strongly negative words when discussing a policy. What might this reveal?
examples.solution: The writer may have a critical or negative attitude toward the policy.

examples.question: What is evidence used for in an argument?
examples.solution: Evidence supports or helps justify the writer’s claim or position.

examples.question: Can an opinion automatically be treated as a fact because the writer states it confidently?
examples.solution: No. Confidence does not make an opinion a verifiable fact.

topics.name: Lexical and Contextual Meaning

objectives: Determine the meaning of words from context
Recognize different meanings of the same word
Select replacements that preserve the original meaning

lesson.title: Lexical and Contextual Meaning
lesson.introduction: Words do not always have one fixed meaning. Their intended meaning depends on the sentence and situation in which they are used.

sections.title: Contextual Meaning
sections.content: Contextual meaning is the meaning a word or expression has in a particular passage. Read the surrounding sentences before choosing an answer.

sections.title: Synonyms
sections.content: A synonym is a word with a similar meaning. In comprehension questions, the best synonym is the one that fits the specific context.

sections.title: Antonyms
sections.content: An antonym has an opposite meaning. The correct opposite must match the sense in which the original word is used.

sections.title: Literal and Figurative Meaning
sections.content: Some expressions have direct meanings while others are used figuratively. Context helps determine which meaning is intended.

sections.title: Multiple Meanings
sections.content: A single word may have several meanings. For example, "bank" can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river. The passage determines the intended meaning.

sections.title: Replacement Questions
sections.content: When asked to replace a word or expression without changing its meaning, choose the option that preserves the meaning of the original sentence in context.

keyPoints: Always interpret words within their context.
The most common dictionary meaning is not always the intended meaning.
Synonyms must fit the context.
Antonyms must match the particular sense being tested.
Expressions may be literal or figurative.
Choose replacements that preserve the original meaning.

examples.question: What should you do when a comprehension question asks for the meaning of a word "as used in the passage"?
examples.solution: Read the surrounding context and determine the meaning intended in that passage.

examples.question: Can the same word have different meanings in different sentences?
examples.solution: Yes. Context determines which meaning is intended.

examples.question: If asked to replace an expression without changing its meaning, what should you check?
examples.solution: Check that the replacement has the same meaning and fits grammatically in the original context.

topics.name: Logical Relationships and Sequence of Ideas
topics.description: This skill involves understanding how ideas in a passage are connected and arranged, including cause and effect, contrast, comparison, sequence, condition and result.
objectives: Follow the sequence of events or arguments
Understand the function of linking words
Identify how one paragraph or idea relates to another

lesson.title: Logical Relationships and Sequence of Ideas
lesson.introduction: Writers connect ideas using logical relationships and linking expressions. Understanding these relationships makes it easier to follow a passage and answer comprehension questions.

sections.title: Cause and Effect
sections.content: A cause explains why something happens, while an effect describes what happens as a result. Words such as "because", "therefore", "since" and "as a result" can signal this relationship.

sections.title: Comparison and Contrast
sections.content: Comparison shows similarities, while contrast highlights differences. Expressions such as "similarly", "however", "whereas" and "on the other hand" can provide clues.

sections.title: Condition and Result
sections.content: A condition describes what must happen for another event or result to occur. Words such as "if", "unless" and "provided that" can signal conditions.

sections.title: Sequence
sections.content: Sequence shows the order in which events or ideas occur. Words such as "first", "then", "afterward", "finally" and "subsequently" can indicate order.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content: Purpose explains why an action is performed. Expressions such as "in order to", "so that" and "for the purpose of" can indicate purpose.

sections.title: Linking Expressions
sections.content: Linking expressions connect sentences and paragraphs. Understanding what a connector means can reveal the relationship between the ideas before and after it.

keyPoints: Look for linking words and expressions.
Distinguish causes from effects.
Recognize similarities and differences.
Identify conditions and their results.
Follow the order of events and arguments.
Use connectors to understand relationships between ideas.

examples.question: In the sentence "He was ill; therefore, he stayed at home", what relationship does "therefore" indicate?
examples.solution: Cause and effect. His illness led to the result that he stayed at home.

examples.question: What relationship does "however" commonly signal?
examples.solution: Contrast or a change in direction between ideas.

examples.question: What does "finally" usually indicate in a passage?
examples.solution: The last stage or point in a sequence.

topics.name: Synonyms
topics.description: Synonyms are words or expressions that have the same or nearly the same meaning in a particular context.
objectives: Choose the word closest in meaning to a given word
Distinguish exact meaning from approximate meaning

lesson.title: Synonyms
lesson.introduction: A synonym is a word that has the same or a similar meaning as another word. In JAMB questions, the correct synonym is the option that best matches the meaning of the word as it is used in the sentence.

sections.title: Meaning of Synonyms
sections.content: Synonyms are words with the same or closely related meanings. They are not always interchangeable because their meanings can depend on context.

sections.title: Context Matters
sections.content: Always examine the sentence before selecting a synonym. A word may have several meanings, and only one meaning may fit the particular sentence.

sections.title: Closest Meaning
sections.content: In examination questions, several options may appear related to the given word. Select the option whose meaning is closest to the meaning intended in the sentence.

sections.title: Common Examples
sections.content: Begin — start; rapid — fast; assist — help; purchase — buy; accurate — correct; difficult — hard; abandon — leave; generous — giving.

sections.title: Avoiding Traps
sections.content: Do not choose an option merely because it sounds familiar. Replace the target word with each option mentally and check which one preserves the original meaning.

keyPoints: A synonym has the same or a closely related meaning.
The sentence context determines the intended meaning.
Choose the closest meaning, not simply a related word.
A word can have different synonyms in different contexts.
Test the option by replacing the original word in the sentence.

examples.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to "rapid": slow, quick, weak, late.
examples.solution: Quick. Rapid means happening or moving very fast.

examples.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to "assist": prevent, help, refuse, delay.
examples.solution: Help. To assist someone means to help them.

examples.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to "abandon": protect, leave, follow, repair.
examples.solution: Leave. To abandon something or someone means to leave it or them behind.

topics.name: Antonyms
topics.description: Antonyms are words or expressions with opposite or contrasting meanings. In JAMB questions, the correct antonym is determined by the meaning of the target word in its sentence.
objectives: Choose the word closest in meaning to the opposite of a given word
Use context to determine the intended meaning
Recognize words formed with negative prefixes
Distinguish true opposites from merely related words

lesson.title: Antonyms
lesson.introduction: An antonym is a word whose meaning contrasts with or is opposite to another word. As with synonyms, context is important because a word may have different meanings in different situations.

sections.title: Meaning of Antonyms
sections.content: Antonyms express contrasting meanings. Examples include hot and cold, early and late, success and failure, and accept and reject.

sections.title: Context Matters
sections.content: The correct opposite depends on the meaning intended in the sentence. Do not select an option simply because it is generally associated with the target word.

sections.title: Negative Prefixes
sections.content: Some opposites are formed by prefixes such as un-, in-, im-, ir- and dis-. Examples include happy/unhappy, possible/impossible and regular/irregular.

sections.title: Closest Opposite
sections.content: In examination questions, select the option that most accurately expresses the opposite meaning intended by the sentence.

sections.title: Avoiding Traps
sections.content: A word can be related to another word without being its opposite. Compare the meanings carefully and use the sentence context.

keyPoints: An antonym expresses an opposite or contrasting meaning.
Context determines the intended meaning.
Not every related word is an antonym.
Negative prefixes can form opposites.
Choose the closest opposite meaning required by the sentence.

examples.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to "ancient": old, modern, historic, traditional.
examples.solution: Modern. Ancient refers to something from a very long time ago, while modern refers to the present or recent times.

examples.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to "expand": increase, enlarge, contract, develop.
examples.solution: Contract. To contract means to become smaller or reduce in size.

examples.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to "generous": kind, selfish, helpful, friendly.
examples.solution: Selfish. A selfish person is unwilling to give or share, contrasting with generosity.

topics.name: Homonyms
topics.description: Homonyms are words that have the same form or pronunciation but different meanings. Understanding their meanings in context is important when answering JAMB Use of English questions.
content: Choosing the correct word in a sentence
objectives: Distinguish between homonyms and related word forms
Use context to determine the intended meaning
Choose the correct word in a sentence

lesson.title: Homonyms
lesson.introduction: Some English words have the same pronunciation or spelling but different meanings. Context helps determine which meaning is intended.

sections.title: Homonyms
sections.content: Homonyms are words that share the same form or sound while having different meanings. Their exact classification can depend on whether the words share spelling, pronunciation or both.

sections.title: Homophones
sections.content: Homophones are words that sound alike but have different meanings and usually different spellings. Examples include right/write, sea/see and flour/flower.

sections.title: Homographs
sections.content: Homographs are words that are spelled the same but have different meanings. Some homographs may also have different pronunciations, depending on their meanings.

sections.title: Context
sections.content: The surrounding words and the meaning of the sentence determine which interpretation is correct. Always read the complete sentence before choosing an answer.

sections.title: Commonly Confused Words
sections.content: Words such as their/there/they’re, your/you’re and principal/principle can cause errors because their forms or meanings are closely related. Learn their meanings and grammatical functions.

keyPoints: Context is essential when distinguishing words with similar forms or sounds.
Homophones sound alike but have different meanings.
Homographs have the same spelling but different meanings.
Do not choose a word based only on pronunciation.
Check both meaning and grammatical use.

examples.question: Choose the correct word: The students were asked to write their names over ___.
examples.solution: There. The correct expression is "over there" when referring to a place.

examples.question: Choose the correct word: I can ___ the music clearly.
examples.solution: Hear. "Hear" means to perceive sound, while "here" refers to a place.

examples.question: Choose the correct word: The school ___ addressed the students.
examples.solution: Principal. A principal is the head of a school, while a principle is a rule or belief.

topics.name: Clause and Sentence Patterns
topics.description: Clauses and sentence patterns describe how words and groups of words are organized to form meaningful English sentences.
objectives: Recognize noun, adjective and adverbial clauses
Identify errors caused by incorrect sentence structure

lesson.title: Clause and Sentence Patterns
lesson.introduction: A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a verb. Clauses combine in different ways to form sentences. Understanding sentence patterns helps you recognize and produce grammatically correct English.

sections.title: Clauses
sections.content: A clause contains a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence, while a dependent clause needs another clause to complete its meaning.

sections.title: Main and Subordinate Clauses
sections.content: The main clause expresses the central statement. A subordinate clause depends on the main clause and may function as a noun, adjective or adverb.

sections.title: Noun Clause
sections.content: A noun clause functions like a noun in a sentence. Example: "What he said was true." The clause "What he said" functions as the subject.

sections.title: Adjective Clause
sections.content: An adjective clause modifies a noun or pronoun. It is often introduced by words such as who, whom, whose, which and that.

sections.title: Adverbial Clause
sections.content: An adverbial clause functions like an adverb and can express time, reason, condition, purpose, contrast and other relationships.

sections.title: Simple Sentence
sections.content: A simple sentence contains one independent clause. It may have a compound subject or compound predicate but still has only one main clause.

sections.title: Compound Sentence
sections.content: A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or appropriate punctuation.

sections.title: Complex Sentence
sections.content: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

sections.title: Compound-Complex Sentence
sections.content: A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns
sections.content: Common patterns include Subject–Verb, Subject–Verb–Object, Subject–Linking Verb–Complement and Subject–Verb–Indirect Object–Direct Object.

keyPoints: A clause contains a subject and a verb.
An independent clause can stand alone.
A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone.
A noun clause functions as a noun.
An adjective clause modifies a noun or pronoun.
An adverbial clause gives information such as time, reason or condition.
A simple sentence has one independent clause.
A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses.
A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

examples.question: Identify the type of sentence: "The boy studied hard, and he passed the examination."
examples.solution: Compound sentence. It contains two independent clauses joined by "and".

examples.question: Identify the dependent clause: "When the rain stopped, the children went outside."
examples.solution: "When the rain stopped" is the dependent clause because it cannot stand alone as a complete statement.

examples.question: Identify the adjective clause: "The student who won the prize was excited."
examples.solution: "Who won the prize" is an adjective clause because it modifies "student".

topics.name: Word Classes
topics.description: Word classes are categories that describe the grammatical functions of words in sentences. Recognizing them helps with correct sentence construction and interpretation.
content: Words that can belong to different classes
objectives: Determine the grammatical class of a word from its context

lesson.title: Word Classes
lesson.introduction: English words perform different grammatical functions. A word’s class is often determined by how it is used in a sentence.

sections.title: Nouns
sections.content: Nouns name people, places, things, animals, ideas or qualities. Examples include teacher, Lagos, book, honesty and freedom.

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.content: Pronouns replace or refer to nouns. Examples include he, she, it, they, we, who and which.

sections.title: Verbs
sections.content: Verbs express actions, events or states. Examples include run, write, become, know and seem.

sections.title: Adjectives
sections.content: Adjectives modify nouns or pronouns by describing qualities, quantities or characteristics. Examples include tall, difficult, several and beautiful.

sections.title: Adverbs
sections.content: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or whole clauses. They may express manner, time, place, frequency or degree.

sections.title: Prepositions
sections.content: Prepositions show relationships between words, often involving place, time, direction or other connections. Examples include in, on, at, under, between and through.

sections.title: Conjunctions
sections.content: Conjunctions connect words, phrases or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or, nor, for, so and yet.

sections.title: Determiners
sections.content: Determiners occur before nouns and help identify or specify them. Examples include a, an, the, this, those, some, many and each.

sections.title: Interjections
sections.content: Interjections express sudden feelings or reactions. Examples include oh, wow, ouch and hey.

sections.title: Context
sections.content: The same word may perform different grammatical functions in different sentences. Always examine how the word is being used rather than relying only on its dictionary meaning.

keyPoints: Nouns name people, places, things, ideas or qualities.
Pronouns replace or refer to nouns.
Verbs express actions, events or states.
Adjectives modify nouns or pronouns.
Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, adverbs or clauses.
Prepositions show relationships between words.
Conjunctions connect words, phrases or clauses.
Determiners help specify nouns.
A word’s grammatical class can depend on its use in context.

examples.question: Identify the word class of "beautiful" in "She wore a beautiful dress."
examples.solution: Adjective. It describes the noun "dress".

examples.question: Identify the word class of "quickly" in "He ran quickly."
examples.solution: Adverb. It modifies the verb "ran" by describing how he ran.

examples.question: Identify the word class of "under" in "The book is under the table."
examples.solution: Preposition. It shows the relationship between "book" and "table".

topics.name: Concord
topics.description: Concord is the grammatical agreement between words in a sentence, especially the agreement between a subject and its verb in number and person.
objectives: Use correct verbs with compound subjects
Apply agreement rules to collective nouns
Apply agreement rules to indefinite pronouns
Choose the grammatically correct option in examination questions

lesson.title: Concord
lesson.introduction: Concord means grammatical agreement between elements in a sentence. In English, the verb normally agrees with its subject in number and person.

sections.title: Basic Subject–Verb Agreement
sections.content: A singular subject generally takes a singular verb, while a plural subject generally takes a plural verb. Example: "The boy runs" and "The boys run."

sections.title: Compound Subjects
sections.content: Subjects joined by "and" generally take a plural verb when they refer to separate people or things. Example: "John and Mary are ready."

sections.title: Either and Neither
sections.content: When either or neither is used as a singular subject, it generally takes a singular verb. In constructions involving either...or or neither...nor, agreement can depend on the subject nearer the verb.

sections.title: Indefinite Pronouns
sections.content: Words such as everyone, everybody, someone, nobody and each are normally treated as singular and therefore take singular verbs.

sections.title: Collective Nouns
sections.content: Collective nouns refer to groups. Their verb agreement can depend on whether the group is treated as a single unit or as individual members, according to the variety and context of English being used.

sections.title: Quantities and Measurements
sections.content: Expressions of amount, distance, time or money may take a singular verb when they are treated as one unit. Example: "Ten kilometres is a long distance."

sections.title: Common Errors
sections.content: Do not allow words between the subject and verb to confuse you. Identify the actual subject first, then choose the verb that agrees with it.

keyPoints: The subject and verb should agree in number and person.
A singular subject normally takes a singular verb.
A plural subject normally takes a plural verb.
Subjects joined by "and" generally take a plural verb.
Everyone, everybody, someone and each are normally singular.
Words between the subject and verb do not change the subject.
Check the actual subject before selecting the verb.

examples.question: Choose the correct option: The boy ___ to school every day. (go/goes)
examples.solution: Goes. "The boy" is singular, so it takes the singular verb "goes".

examples.question: Choose the correct option: The students ___ ready for the examination. (is/are)
examples.solution: Are. "The students" is plural, so it takes "are".

examples.question: Choose the correct option: Everyone in the class ___ present. (was/were)
examples.solution: Was. "Everyone" is treated as a singular subject.

topics.name: Tenses
topics.description: Tense shows the time of an action, event or state. Correct tense usage helps establish when something happens, happened or will happen.
objectives: Distinguish simple, continuous and perfect forms
Choose the correct tense from context
Identify and correct common tense errors

lesson.title: Tenses
lesson.introduction: Tense helps indicate when an action or state occurs. In JAMB questions, the correct tense is often determined by time expressions, surrounding verbs and the relationship between events.

sections.title: Simple Present
sections.content: The simple present is commonly used for habits, routines, facts and general truths. Example: "She reads every evening."

sections.title: Simple Past
sections.content: The simple past describes completed actions or states in the past. Example: "They visited Aba yesterday."

sections.title: Simple Future
sections.content: Future meaning can be expressed with forms such as will and be going to, depending on the intended meaning and context.

sections.title: Continuous Forms
sections.content: Continuous forms describe actions in progress at a particular time. Examples include "is reading", "was reading" and "will be reading".

sections.title: Perfect Forms
sections.content: Perfect forms connect an earlier action or state with a later point in time. Examples include "has finished", "had finished" and "will have finished".

sections.title: Sequence of Tenses
sections.content: When several events are described, the tense choices should clearly show their relationships in time. Time expressions and conjunctions can help establish the sequence.

sections.title: Tense Consistency
sections.content: Avoid unnecessary changes between past, present and future forms. The tense should remain consistent unless the meaning requires a change.

sections.title: Common Errors
sections.content: Watch for incorrect verb forms, unnecessary tense changes and disagreement between time expressions and the selected verb tense.

keyPoints: Tense indicates the time of an action, event or state.
Use simple present for many habits and general truths.
Use simple past for completed past events.
Continuous forms describe actions in progress.
Perfect forms connect an earlier event to another point in time.
Use context and time expressions to determine the correct tense.
Maintain tense consistency unless a change is required by the meaning.

examples.question: Choose the correct option: She ___ to school every morning. (go/goes)
examples.solution: Goes. The sentence describes a regular habit, so the simple present is appropriate.

examples.question: Choose the correct option: They ___ the match yesterday. (win/won)
examples.solution: Won. "Yesterday" indicates a completed event in the past.

examples.question: Choose the correct option: By the time we arrived, the train ___. (left/had left)
examples.solution: Had left. The train left before another past event, our arrival.

topics.name: Punctuation and Spelling
topics.description: Punctuation and spelling are essential parts of written English. Correct punctuation helps communicate meaning clearly, while correct spelling ensures that words are accurately represented.

lesson.title: Punctuation and Spelling
lesson.introduction: Correct punctuation and spelling make written communication clear and accurate. JAMB questions may require you to identify the correctly written or punctuated form of a sentence.

sections.title: Full Stop
sections.content: A full stop normally ends a complete declarative sentence.

sections.title: Comma
sections.content: A comma can separate items in a list, introductory elements, or parts of a sentence where appropriate. It should not normally be used to join two complete sentences by itself.

sections.title: Question Mark
sections.content: A question mark is used at the end of a direct question.

sections.title: Exclamation Mark
sections.content: An exclamation mark can indicate strong emotion, surprise or emphasis.

sections.title: Colon and Semicolon
sections.content: A colon can introduce an explanation, list or example. A semicolon can link closely related independent clauses or separate complex items in a list.

sections.title: Apostrophe
sections.content: An apostrophe is used in contractions and in certain possessive forms. For example, "do not" becomes "don’t", while "the boy’s book" indicates possession.

sections.title: Capitalization
sections.content: Capital letters are used at the beginning of sentences and for proper nouns and other cases where standard English requires them.

sections.title: Spelling
sections.content: Pay attention to commonly confused spellings such as accept/except, advice/advise, principal/principle and separate/separate. Always check the meaning and form required by the sentence.

keyPoints: Punctuation can change or clarify meaning.
Use a full stop to end a complete statement.
Use a question mark for a direct question.
Use commas appropriately rather than joining complete sentences with a comma alone.
Apostrophes have specific uses in contractions and possession.
Use capital letters where standard English requires them.
Check spelling carefully, especially for commonly confused words.

examples.question: Which is correctly punctuated: "Where are you going?" or "Where are you going."?
examples.solution: “Where are you going?” is correct because it is a direct question.

examples.question: Choose the correct word: The school ___ addressed the students. (principal/principle)
examples.solution: Principal. A principal can be the head of a school, while a principle is a rule or belief.

examples.question: Which form shows possession: "the girls books" or "the girl’s book"?
examples.solution: “The girl’s book” correctly uses the apostrophe to show possession.

topics.name: Idioms and Expressions
topics.description: Idioms and expressions are phrases whose meanings may not be understood by interpreting every word literally. JAMB questions often test their meanings in context.
objectives: Determine the meaning of an expression from context
Choose the option closest in meaning to an idiom

lesson.title: Idioms and Expressions
lesson.introduction: An idiom is an expression whose overall meaning may differ from the literal meanings of the individual words. Understanding the context is essential when interpreting idioms.

sections.title: Idioms
sections.content: An idiom is a fixed or relatively fixed expression with a meaning that cannot always be understood literally. For example, "break the ice" can mean to make people feel more comfortable in a new or tense situation.

sections.title: Literal and Figurative Meaning
sections.content: A literal meaning is the direct meaning of the words, while a figurative meaning communicates an idea beyond the literal words. Idioms generally require interpretation of their figurative meaning.

sections.title: Context
sections.content: The surrounding sentence or passage helps determine the intended meaning of an expression. Do not interpret an idiom without considering how it is being used.

sections.title: Common Expressions
sections.content: Examples include "once in a blue moon" meaning very rarely, "hit the nail on the head" meaning to identify something accurately, and "under the weather" meaning to feel unwell.

sections.title: Choosing the Correct Meaning
sections.content: In examination questions, select the option that best expresses the meaning of the complete expression in its context rather than the literal meaning of individual words.

keyPoints: Idioms often have figurative meanings.
Do not interpret idioms literally unless the context clearly requires it.
Context is important when determining meaning.
Choose the option closest to the meaning of the complete expression.
Learn common expressions and understand how they are used.

examples.question: What does "once in a blue moon" mean?
examples.solution: Very rarely.

examples.question: What does "hit the nail on the head" mean?
examples.solution: To describe or identify something accurately.

examples.question: What does "under the weather" mean?
examples.solution: To feel unwell.

topics.name: Sentence Completion
topics.description: Sentence completion tests the ability to select the word or expression that makes a sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.
objectives: Use context to complete sentences correctly
Select words that fit the intended meaning
Eliminate grammatically or logically unsuitable options

lesson.title: Sentence Completion
lesson.introduction: Sentence completion questions require you to choose the word or expression that best completes a sentence. The correct answer must fit both the grammar and the meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Use the Context
sections.content: Read the entire sentence before considering the options. The surrounding words often provide clues about the required meaning.

sections.title: Check Grammar
sections.content: The selected option must agree with the subject and fit the tense, number, word class and structure required by the sentence.

sections.title: Check Meaning
sections.content: An option can be grammatically possible but still wrong because it does not make sense in the context. Always consider both grammar and meaning.

sections.title: Prepositions
sections.content: Some words naturally occur with particular prepositions. Learn common combinations such as "interested in", "depend on" and "responsible for".

sections.title: Collocations
sections.content: Collocations are words that commonly occur together. Correct sentence completion often depends on choosing the word that forms the natural combination.

sections.title: Elimination
sections.content: Remove options that clearly violate grammar, meaning or context. Comparing the remaining options can make the correct answer easier to identify.

keyPoints: Read the complete sentence first.
Check grammar and meaning together.
Pay attention to tense and concord.
Check required prepositions.
Consider common word combinations.
Eliminate options that do not fit the context.

examples.question: The students ___ their assignments before the teacher arrived. (complete/completed/had completed/completing)
examples.solution: Had completed. The assignment was completed before another past event, the teacher’s arrival.

examples.question: She is interested ___ learning French. (at/in/on/for)
examples.solution: In. The correct collocation is "interested in".

examples.question: The manager is responsible ___ the project. (to/for/with/at)
examples.solution: For. The correct expression is "responsible for".

topics.name: Mood, Aspect, Degree and Question Tags
topics.description: English grammar uses mood, aspect, degree and question tags to express different meanings, relationships and attitudes in sentences.
objectives: Recognize indicative, imperative and subjunctive constructions
Identify simple, continuous and perfect aspects
Distinguish positive, comparative and superlative degrees
Apply these grammatical structures correctly in context

lesson.title: Mood, Aspect, Degree and Question Tags
lesson.introduction: These grammatical features help speakers and writers express statements, commands, conditions, comparison, time relationships and requests for confirmation.

sections.title: Mood
sections.content: Mood refers to the form of a verb or sentence used to express the speaker’s purpose or attitude. Common types include indicative, imperative and subjunctive.

sections.title: Indicative Mood
sections.content: The indicative mood is commonly used for statements and questions about facts or situations. Example: "She lives in Aba."

sections.title: Imperative Mood
sections.content: The imperative mood is commonly used for commands, instructions or requests. Example: "Close the door."

sections.title: Subjunctive Mood
sections.content: The subjunctive is used in certain formal expressions, wishes, recommendations and hypothetical situations. Example: "It is important that he be present."

sections.title: Aspect
sections.content: Aspect shows how an action or situation relates to time, such as whether it is viewed as ongoing or completed.

sections.title: Continuous Aspect
sections.content: Continuous forms present an action as ongoing. Examples include "is reading" and "was reading".

sections.title: Perfect Aspect
sections.content: Perfect forms indicate a completed action or state viewed in relation to another time. Examples include "has finished" and "had finished".

sections.title: Degree
sections.content: Adjectives and some adverbs can express positive, comparative and superlative degrees.

sections.title: Positive Degree
sections.content: The positive degree expresses a quality without making a comparison. Example: "tall".

sections.title: Comparative Degree
sections.content: The comparative degree compares two people or things. Examples include "taller" and "more interesting".

sections.title: Superlative Degree
sections.content: The superlative degree expresses the highest or lowest degree among three or more. Examples include "tallest" and "most interesting".

sections.title: Question Tags
sections.content: A question tag is a short question added to a statement, usually to seek confirmation. Example: "She is coming, isn’t she?"

keyPoints: Indicative mood is commonly used for statements and questions.
Imperative mood is used for commands and instructions.
Subjunctive forms occur in certain formal, hypothetical and recommendation structures.
Aspect shows how an action relates to time.
Continuous aspect presents an action as ongoing.
Perfect aspect presents an action in relation to another point in time.
Positive, comparative and superlative are the main degrees of comparison.
Question tags normally reflect the auxiliary verb and polarity of the statement.

examples.question: Identify the mood: "Please close the window."
examples.solution: Imperative mood. The sentence gives a request or instruction.

examples.question: Choose the correct form: "John is ___ than Peter." (tall/taller/tallest)
examples.solution: Taller. The sentence compares two people.

examples.question: Complete the question tag: "She is your sister, ___?"
examples.solution: Isn’t she? The statement is positive, so the usual tag is negative.

topics.name: Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage
topics.description: English expressions can be used in their ordinary, figurative or idiomatic senses. Understanding the intended sense of an expression is essential for interpreting language correctly.
objectives: Choose the correct interpretation of an expression

lesson.title: Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage
lesson.introduction: Words and expressions can communicate their direct meaning or a meaning that goes beyond the literal words. Context helps determine which sense is intended.

sections.title: Ordinary Usage
sections.content: Ordinary usage refers to words being used in their common or direct sense. Example: "The boy opened the door." The word "opened" has its ordinary meaning.

sections.title: Figurative Usage
sections.content: Figurative language uses words in a non-literal way to create a particular image, comparison or effect. Example: "The news broke his heart" does not mean that his physical heart was broken.

sections.title: Idiomatic Usage
sections.content: Idiomatic expressions have established meanings that may not be predictable from the individual words. Their meanings must often be learned and understood from context.

sections.title: Context
sections.content: The surrounding words and situation determine whether an expression is being used literally, figuratively or idiomatically.

sections.title: Figures of Speech
sections.content: Common figures of speech include simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole and irony. Recognizing these devices can help you interpret figurative expressions.

keyPoints: Ordinary usage generally expresses a direct meaning.
Figurative usage communicates a meaning beyond the literal words.
Idioms have established meanings that may not be literal.
Context is essential when interpreting expressions.
Do not assume every expression should be interpreted literally.

examples.question: In "The baby is sleeping on the bed", is the expression ordinary or figurative?
examples.solution: Ordinary. The words are being used in their direct meanings.

examples.question: What does "He has a heart of stone" suggest?
examples.solution: It figuratively suggests that he is emotionally hard or unfeeling.

examples.question: What does "She spilled the beans" mean in ordinary English usage?
examples.solution: As an idiom, it means that she revealed secret information.

topics.name: Vowels
topics.description: Vowel sounds are produced without complete obstruction of the airflow. Understanding vowel sounds helps candidates distinguish words that differ in pronunciation.
objectives: Distinguish short and long vowel sounds
Distinguish words based on their vowel sounds

lesson.title: Vowels
lesson.introduction: Vowel sounds are produced when air passes through the vocal tract without complete blockage. Different vowel sounds can distinguish words with otherwise similar pronunciation.

sections.title: Vowel Sounds
sections.content: Vowels are speech sounds produced without complete obstruction of airflow. The position of the tongue and lips affects the sound produced.

sections.title: Short and Long Vowels
sections.content: English has vowel contrasts that are commonly described as short and long. Candidates should learn to recognize these differences in spoken words.

sections.title: Vowel Symbols
sections.content: The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) uses symbols to represent speech sounds. Learning common English vowel symbols helps with pronunciation questions.

sections.title: Vowel Contrast
sections.content: A change in vowel sound can change the meaning of a word. For example, "ship" and "sheep" contain different vowel sounds.

sections.title: Spelling and Pronunciation
sections.content: English spelling does not always correspond directly to pronunciation. When answering oral-form questions, focus on the actual sound rather than simply comparing written letters.

keyPoints: Vowels are produced without complete obstruction of airflow.
English contains several different vowel sounds.
Vowel sounds can distinguish words.
Spelling does not always indicate pronunciation.
IPA symbols can represent vowel sounds precisely.

examples.question: Do "ship" and "sheep" contain the same vowel sound?
examples.solution: No. The vowel sounds are different.

examples.question: When comparing vowel sounds in an oral English question, should you focus mainly on spelling?
examples.solution: No. Focus on the actual pronunciation of the words.

topics.name: Consonants
topics.description: Consonant sounds are produced with some degree of obstruction or narrowing of the airflow. Candidates need to recognize consonant sounds and distinguish words that differ because of them.
objectives: Distinguish words based on their consonant sounds

lesson.title: Consonants
