lesson.introduction: Consonant sounds are produced when the airflow is blocked, restricted or narrowed at some point in the vocal tract. Consonants may differ in voicing, place and manner of articulation.

sections.title: Consonant Sounds
sections.content: Consonants involve some degree of obstruction or narrowing of the airflow. Examples include the sounds represented by b, t, k, m, s and f.

sections.title: Voiced and Voiceless Consonants
sections.content: Voiced consonants are produced with vibration of the vocal folds, while voiceless consonants are produced without this vibration. For example, /b/ is voiced while /p/ is voiceless.

sections.title: Place of Articulation
sections.content: Place of articulation refers to where the airflow is obstructed or narrowed. Common places include the lips, teeth, alveolar region and the back of the mouth.

sections.title: Manner of Articulation
sections.content: Manner of articulation describes how the airflow is affected. Common manners include stops, fricatives, affricates, nasals and approximants.

sections.title: Consonant Contrast
sections.content: Changing one consonant sound can change the meaning of a word. For example, "fan" and "van" differ in their initial consonant sounds.

sections.title: Spelling and Pronunciation
sections.content: Written letters do not always correspond to one particular sound. Oral English questions should therefore be answered by comparing pronunciation rather than spelling alone.

keyPoints: Consonants involve some obstruction or narrowing of airflow.
Consonants can be voiced or voiceless.
Place of articulation describes where a sound is produced.
Manner of articulation describes how airflow is affected.
A consonant change can change the meaning of a word.
Spelling does not always directly represent pronunciation.

examples.question: Are /b/ and /p/ produced in exactly the same way?
examples.solution: No. They are both bilabial stops, but /b/ is voiced while /p/ is voiceless.

examples.question: Do "fan" and "van" begin with the same consonant sound?
examples.solution: No. Their initial consonant sounds are different.

examples.question: When answering an oral English question, should you rely only on the written letters?
examples.solution: No. Compare the actual sounds represented by the words.

topics.name: Rhymes and Homophones
topics.description: Rhyming words share similar ending sounds, while homophones are words that have the same or very similar pronunciation but different meanings and often different spellings.
objectives: Compare the ending sounds of words
Distinguish homophones by meaning and spelling

lesson.title: Rhymes and Homophones
lesson.introduction: Rhymes and homophones are important parts of spoken English. JAMB may test your ability to recognize words that share similar sounds or words that sound alike but have different meanings.

sections.title: Rhymes
sections.content: Words rhyme when their stressed ending sounds are sufficiently alike. For example, "light" and "night" rhyme because they share the same ending sound.

sections.title: End Sounds
sections.content: When identifying a rhyme, focus on the sounds from the stressed vowel to the end of the word rather than simply comparing spelling.

sections.title: Homophones
sections.content: Homophones are words that sound alike but have different meanings and usually different spellings. Examples include "right/write", "sea/see" and "pair/pear".

sections.title: Context
sections.content: Because homophones can sound alike, their meaning must be determined from the sentence in which they occur.

sections.title: Spelling and Sound
sections.content: Words that rhyme or sound alike do not necessarily have the same spelling. Oral English questions should therefore focus on pronunciation rather than letters alone.

keyPoints: Rhyming words share similar ending sounds.
Rhyming is based on sound, not necessarily spelling.
Homophones sound alike but have different meanings.
Context helps distinguish homophones.
Always compare pronunciation when answering Oral Forms questions.

examples.question: Which word rhymes with "light": late, night, lot, let?
examples.solution: Night. "Light" and "night" share the same ending sound.

examples.question: Choose the correct word: I can ___ the birds singing. (hear/here)
examples.solution: Hear. "Hear" means to perceive sound, while "here" refers to a place.

examples.question: Are "sea" and "see" homophones?
examples.solution: Yes. They have the same pronunciation but different meanings and spellings.

topics.name: Word Stress
topics.description: Word stress is the emphasis placed on a particular syllable when a word is pronounced. Correct stress helps distinguish words and makes spoken English clearer.
objectives: Recognize stress patterns in monosyllabic words
Recognize stress patterns in polysyllabic words
Recognize common stress patterns in English words

lesson.title: Word Stress
lesson.introduction: Word stress refers to the greater prominence given to one syllable in a word. Prominence can involve features such as greater loudness, length, pitch or clarity of the vowel.

sections.title: Stressed and Unstressed Syllables
sections.content: In a word with more than one syllable, one syllable is normally more prominent than the others. The prominent syllable carries the primary stress.

sections.title: Monosyllabic Words
sections.content: A monosyllabic word has only one syllable. Since there is only one syllable, there is no choice between multiple syllables for primary word stress.

sections.title: Polysyllabic Words
sections.content: Polysyllabic words contain two or more syllables. The position of the primary stress must be learned and recognized as part of the pronunciation of the word.

sections.title: Stress Marks
sections.content: In phonetic transcription, primary stress is commonly marked with ˈ before the stressed syllable. For example, the pronunciation of "about" can be represented with stress on the second syllable.

sections.title: Stress in Related Words
sections.content: Some related words can have different stress patterns. Changes in stress can occur when words change form or when related noun, verb or adjective forms are used.

sections.title: Exam Technique
sections.content: When comparing words, listen for or identify the syllable receiving the strongest prominence. Do not assume that spelling tells you where the stress falls.

keyPoints: Word stress is the prominence given to a syllable.
Monosyllabic words contain one syllable.
Polysyllabic words contain two or more syllables.
Primary stress marks the most prominent syllable.
Spelling alone does not always show stress placement.
Stress patterns must often be learned as part of pronunciation.

examples.question: How many syllables does the word "book" have?
examples.solution: One syllable. It is therefore a monosyllabic word.

examples.question: Which part of a polysyllabic word receives primary stress?
examples.solution: One syllable is normally more prominent than the others and receives the primary stress.

examples.question: Should you rely only on spelling to determine word stress?
examples.solution: No. Stress is a feature of pronunciation and should be learned or checked from the spoken form.

topics.name: Intonation and Emphatic Stress
topics.description: Intonation refers to the pattern of pitch movement in spoken language. Emphatic stress places normal stress on particular words to give them special emphasis.
content: Changes in meaning caused by emphasis
objectives: Recognize intonation in statements and questions
Understand how emphasis can affect meaning
Identify correct accentuation in connected speech

lesson.title: Intonation and Emphatic Stress
lesson.introduction: Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance. Emphatic stress occurs when normal stress is placed on a particular word to make it more prominent and emphasize its meaning.

sections.title: Intonation
sections.content: Intonation is the variation in pitch during speech. Different intonation patterns can help communicate whether a speaker is making a statement, asking a question or expressing an attitude.

sections.title: Rising Intonation
sections.content: Rising intonation involves the pitch moving upward toward the end of an utterance. It commonly occurs in some questions and when a speaker indicates that an utterance is incomplete or expects continuation.

sections.title: Falling Intonation
sections.content: Falling intonation involves the pitch moving downward toward the end of an utterance. It commonly occurs in many statements and some types of questions.

sections.title: Emphatic Stress
sections.content: Emphatic stress gives extra prominence to a word in an utterance. The emphasis can draw attention to a particular piece of information or create a contrast.

sections.title: Meaning and Emphasis
sections.content: Changing which word receives emphatic stress can change what the speaker is highlighting. In examination questions, identify the word that is receiving special prominence and consider what information it emphasizes.

sections.title: Connected Speech
sections.content: In connected speech, words are pronounced as part of a continuous utterance. Stress and intonation work together to communicate meaning clearly.

keyPoints: Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement in speech.
Rising and falling intonation can serve different communicative purposes.
Emphatic stress gives special prominence to a word.
Changing the stressed word can change the information being emphasized.
Oral English questions focus on pronunciation rather than spelling alone.

examples.question: What is intonation?
examples.solution: Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across a spoken utterance.

examples.question: What is emphatic stress?
examples.solution: It is the placement of normal stress on a word to give that word special emphasis.

examples.question: Can changing the word receiving emphasis affect the meaning of an utterance?
examples.solution: Yes. Different words can be emphasized to highlight different information or create contrast.

topics.name: Number Bases
topics.description: Operations in different number bases from 2 to 10 and conversion from one base to another, including fractional parts.
objectives: Perform the four basic operations: multiplication, addition, subtraction and division.
Convert one number base to another.
content: Conversion of numbers from one base to another
Operations involving numbers in different bases

lesson.title: Number Bases
lesson.introduction: A number base is a system used to represent numbers using a fixed set of digits. In base 10, which we normally use, the digits are 0 to 9. Other bases use fewer or more digits depending on the base.

sections.title: Understanding Place Value
sections.content: In any number base, the value of a digit depends on its position. Each position represents a power of the base.

sections.title: Converting From Another Base to Base 10
sections.content: To convert a number to base 10, multiply each digit by the appropriate power of the original base and add the results.

sections.title: Converting From Base 10 to Another Base
sections.content: Repeatedly divide the base-10 number by the new base. Record the remainders and read them from bottom to top.

sections.title: Operations in Other Bases
sections.content: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division can be performed in another base. The result must be written using only digits allowed in that base.

sections.title: Fractional Parts
sections.content: Numbers with fractional parts can also be represented in different bases. Conversion uses powers of the base on the fractional positions.

sections.title: Modulo Arithmetic
sections.content: Modulo arithmetic deals with remainders after division. For example, 17 modulo 5 is 2 because 17 divided by 5 leaves a remainder of 2.

keyPoints: Base 2 uses digits 0 and 1.
Base 5 uses digits 0 to 4.
Base 10 uses digits 0 to 9.
The rightmost whole-number position has power 0.
Each position to the left increases the power by 1.
Each position to the right of the radix point uses negative powers.
When converting to base 10, use powers of the original base.
When converting from base 10, repeated division gives the remainders.

examples.question: Convert 1011₂ to base 10.
Convert 13₁₀ to base 2.
examples.solution: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1. Reading the remainders from bottom to top gives 1101₂.

topics.name: Fractions, Decimals, Approximations and Percentages
topics.description: This topic covers fractions, decimals, percentages and the approximation of numbers used in mathematical calculations and everyday problems.
objectives: Perform operations involving fractions and decimals
Convert numbers between fractions, decimals and percentages
Apply approximation and estimation in calculations
Express numbers to specified decimal places and significant figures
content: Decimal fractions and their conversion to ordinary fractions
Conversion between fractions, decimals and percentages

lesson.title: Fractions, Decimals, Approximations & Percentages
lesson.introduction: Fractions, decimals and percentages are different ways of representing quantities. Understanding how to convert between them and how to approximate numbers is essential for solving many JAMB Mathematics problems.

sections.title: Fractions
sections.content: A fraction represents part of a whole and is written as a numerator over a denominator. Fractions can be proper, improper or mixed numbers. They can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided using the appropriate rules.

sections.title: Decimals
sections.content: A decimal represents a number using place values based on powers of ten. For example, 0.5 represents five tenths. Decimals can be converted to fractions and percentages.

sections.title: Percentages
sections.content: A percentage means a quantity expressed out of 100. To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100. To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100.

sections.title: Approximation
sections.content: Approximation replaces a number with a nearby value that is easier to use. Common forms include rounding to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.

sections.title: Estimation
sections.content: Estimation uses suitably rounded values to obtain a quick approximate answer. It is useful for checking whether a calculated answer is reasonable.

keyPoints: A percentage is a fraction expressed out of 100.
To convert a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100%.
To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100.
Decimal places count digits after the decimal point.
Significant figures begin with the first non-zero digit.
When rounding, inspect the digit immediately after the required position.
Estimation gives an approximate value rather than an exact value.

examples.question: Convert 3/4 to a percentage.
Convert 0.35 to a percentage.
Round 47.386 to 2 decimal places.
examples.solution: The hundredths digit is 8 and the next digit is 6, so the 8 is increased to 9. Therefore, 47.386 ≈ 47.39.

topics.name: Indices, Logarithms and Surds
topics.description: This topic covers indices, logarithms and surds, including their laws, simplification and application to mathematical problems.
objectives: Apply the laws of indices to simplify expressions
Apply the laws of logarithms in calculations
Convert logarithms from one base to another
Use the relationship between indices and logarithms
content: Expressions involving positive, zero and negative indices

lesson.title: Indices, Logarithms & Surds
lesson.introduction: Indices, logarithms and surds are closely connected ideas used to simplify expressions and solve mathematical problems. Understanding their laws makes many JAMB calculations much easier.

sections.title: Laws of Indices
sections.content: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the indices. When dividing powers with the same base, subtract the indices. A power raised to another power has its indices multiplied.

sections.title: Zero and Negative Indices
sections.content: Any non-zero number raised to the power zero is 1. A negative index represents the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power.

sections.title: Fractional Indices
sections.content: A fractional index can represent a root as well as a power. For example, a^(1/2) represents the square root of a.

sections.title: Standard Form
sections.content: Standard form expresses a number as a × 10^n, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. It is useful for very large and very small numbers.

sections.title: Logarithms
sections.content: A logarithm tells us the power to which a base must be raised to produce a given number. The laws of logarithms allow products, quotients and powers to be handled more conveniently.

sections.title: Surds
sections.content: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be simplified to a rational number. Surds can be simplified and combined using the laws of multiplication and addition.

sections.title: Rationalization
sections.content: Rationalization removes a surd from the denominator of a fraction. This is commonly done by multiplying by a suitable surd or conjugate.

keyPoints: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n)
a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n), for a ≠ 0
(a^m)^n = a^(mn)
a^0 = 1, for a ≠ 0
a^(1/n) represents the nth root of a
Standard form has a coefficient from 1 up to but not including 10
log_a(xy) = log_a(x) + log_a(y)
log_a(x/y) = log_a(x) - log_a(y)
log_a(x^n) = n log_a(x)

examples.question: Simplify 2^3 × 2^4.
examples.solution: Since the bases are the same, add the indices: 2^(3+4) = 2^7 = 128.

examples.question: Simplify 5^7 ÷ 5^3.
examples.solution: Subtract the indices: 5^(7-3) = 5^4 = 625.

examples.question: Express 0.00045 in standard form.
examples.solution: Move the decimal point four places to the right: 0.00045 = 4.5 × 10^(-4).

examples.question: Simplify √50.
Rationalize 1/√2.
examples.solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by √2: (1 × √2)/(√2 × √2) = √2/2.

topics.name: Sets
topics.description: Sets are collections of well-defined objects. This topic covers types of sets, operations on sets, set notation, cardinality and the use of Venn diagrams to solve problems.
objectives: Identify different types of sets, including empty, universal, complement, subset, finite, infinite and disjoint sets
Represent sets using appropriate symbols and notation
Perform operations involving union, intersection, complement and difference
Solve problems involving the cardinality of sets
Use set symbols correctly in mathematical statements
Use Venn diagrams to solve problems involving up to three sets
content: Types of sets: empty, universal, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent, subsets and disjoint sets
Applications of Venn diagrams involving up to three sets

lesson.title: Sets
lesson.introduction: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The objects in a set are called elements or members. Sets provide a useful way of organizing information and solving problems involving groups of objects.

sections.title: What Is a Set?
sections.content: A set is usually written using braces. For example, A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. The numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 are elements of A. The symbol ∈ means “is an element of”, while ∉ means “is not an element of”.

sections.title: Types of Sets
sections.content: An empty set has no elements. A finite set has a definite number of elements, while an infinite set has infinitely many elements. A universal set contains all objects under consideration. A subset is a set whose elements are all contained in another set. Two sets are disjoint when they have no common element.

sections.title: Set Notation
sections.content: Sets can be described by listing their elements or by stating a rule that the elements satisfy. Symbols such as ∈, ∉, ⊂, ⊆ and U are commonly used when working with sets.

sections.title: Union of Sets
sections.content: The union of A and B, written A ∪ B, contains every element that belongs to A, B, or both. An element is listed only once.

sections.title: Intersection of Sets
sections.content: The intersection of A and B, written A ∩ B, contains only the elements common to both sets.

sections.title: Complement of a Set
sections.content: The complement of A contains all elements in the universal set that are not in A. It is commonly written as A′ or Aᶜ.

sections.title: Difference of Sets
sections.content: A − B contains elements that belong to A but do not belong to B.

sections.title: Cardinality
sections.content: The cardinality of a set is the number of elements in the set. It is written as n(A). For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

sections.title: Venn Diagrams
sections.content: A Venn diagram represents sets using circles inside a rectangle representing the universal set. Overlapping regions represent common elements. Venn diagrams can be used to organize information and solve problems involving up to three sets.

sections.title: Three-Set Problems
sections.content: When three sets are involved, the Venn diagram has regions representing individual sets, pairwise intersections and the intersection of all three sets. Carefully placing the information in the correct regions allows the remaining values to be calculated.

keyPoints: A set contains well-defined elements.
The empty set contains no elements.
A subset contains only elements found in another set.
A ∪ B means union.
A ∩ B means intersection.
A′ represents the complement of A relative to the universal set.
A − B contains elements in A that are not in B.
n(A) represents the cardinality of A.
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
Venn diagrams can be used to solve problems involving up to three sets.

examples.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}, find A ∪ B.
examples.solution: The union contains every element in either set: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

examples.question: Using the same sets, find A ∩ B.
examples.solution: The common elements are 3 and 4. Therefore, A ∩ B = {3, 4}.

examples.question: If n(A) = 20, n(B) = 15 and n(A ∩ B) = 5, find n(A ∪ B).
If U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and A = {2, 4, 6}, find A′.
examples.solution: A′ contains the elements of U that are not in A. Therefore, A′ = {1, 3, 5}.

topics.name: Polynomials
topics.description: Polynomials are algebraic expressions involving variables and constants combined using addition, subtraction and multiplication. This topic covers polynomial operations, factorization, equations and related applications.
objectives: Use relationships between roots and coefficients

lesson.title: Polynomials
lesson.introduction: A polynomial is an algebraic expression made up of terms containing constants and variables raised to non-negative integer powers. Polynomials are important because they provide a systematic way to simplify expressions and solve equations.

sections.title: Understanding Polynomials
sections.content: A polynomial can contain one or more terms. For example, 3x² + 5x − 2 is a quadratic polynomial. The highest power of the variable determines its degree.

sections.title: Operations on Polynomials
sections.content: Like terms can be combined when adding or subtracting polynomials. Polynomial multiplication is carried out by multiplying each term in one expression by each term in the other.

sections.title: Expansion
sections.content: Expansion removes brackets by applying multiplication. For example, (x + 2)(x + 3) becomes x² + 5x + 6.

sections.title: Factorization
sections.content: Factorization expresses a polynomial as a product of simpler expressions. Common methods include taking out common factors, grouping terms and factorizing quadratic expressions.

sections.title: Remainder Theorem
sections.content: If a polynomial f(x) is divided by x − a, the remainder is f(a). This provides a quick way to find the remainder without performing full polynomial division.

sections.title: Factor Theorem
sections.content: If f(a) = 0, then x − a is a factor of f(x). The theorem can therefore be used to test possible factors and solve polynomial equations.

sections.title: Quadratic Equations
sections.content: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a is not zero. Quadratic equations can be solved by factorization, completing the square or using the quadratic formula.

sections.title: Roots and Coefficients
sections.content: For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β, α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. These relationships allow problems involving roots to be solved without finding the roots directly.

keyPoints: The degree of a polynomial is its highest power.
Like terms can be collected during addition and subtraction.
Polynomial multiplication requires every term to be multiplied.
Factorization reverses expansion.
For division by x − a, the remainder is f(a).
If f(a) = 0, then x − a is a factor.
A quadratic has the general form ax² + bx + c = 0.
For roots α and β of ax² + bx + c = 0, α + β = −b/a.
For the same equation, αβ = c/a.

examples.question: Expand (x + 2)(x + 3).
examples.solution: Multiply each term: x(x + 3) + 2(x + 3) = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6.

examples.question: Factorize x² + 5x + 6.
examples.solution: Find two numbers whose product is 6 and whose sum is 5. They are 2 and 3. Therefore x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3).

examples.question: Find the remainder when f(x) = x² + 3x + 2 is divided by x − 1.
examples.solution: By the remainder theorem, substitute x = 1: f(1) = 1² + 3(1) + 2 = 6. The remainder is 6.

examples.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
examples.solution: Factorize: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = 2 or x = 3.

topics.name: Variation
topics.description: Variation describes how one quantity changes in relation to another. It includes direct, inverse, joint and partial variation and their applications to mathematical problems.
objectives: Form variation equations from given information

lesson.title: Variation
lesson.introduction: Variation describes a relationship between quantities. One quantity may increase or decrease as another quantity changes. The main forms are direct, inverse, joint and partial variation.

sections.title: Direct Variation
sections.content: When y varies directly as x, their ratio remains constant. This is written as y ∝ x, which gives y = kx, where k is the constant of variation.

sections.title: Finding the Constant
sections.content: If the values of x and y are known, substitute them into y = kx to find k. Once k is known, the equation can be used to find other values.

sections.title: Inverse Variation
sections.content: When y varies inversely as x, y is proportional to the reciprocal of x. This is written as y ∝ 1/x, giving y = k/x or xy = k.

sections.title: Joint Variation
sections.content: When a quantity varies jointly as two or more quantities, it is proportional to their product. For example, if y varies jointly as x and z, then y = kxz.

sections.title: Partial Variation
sections.content: Partial variation occurs when a quantity varies directly with one variable while also having a constant term. A common form is y = ax + b.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Variation can be used to model relationships in areas such as distance, time, cost, pressure, speed and other quantities that depend on one or more variables.

keyPoints: Direct variation: y = kx.
Inverse variation: y = k/x.
For inverse variation, xy = k.
Joint variation may have the form y = kxz.
Partial variation commonly has the form y = ax + b.
k represents the constant of variation.
Always use the given values to determine the constant before solving for an unknown.

examples.question: If y varies directly as x and y = 12 when x = 4, find y when x = 10.
examples.solution: Since y = kx, 12 = 4k, so k = 3. Therefore y = 3(10) = 30.

examples.question: If y varies inversely as x and y = 6 when x = 4, find y when x = 8.
examples.solution: Since xy = k, k = 4 × 6 = 24. When x = 8, y = 24/8 = 3.

examples.question: If y varies jointly as x and z, and y = 24 when x = 3 and z = 4, find y when x = 5 and z = 2.
examples.solution: y = kxz. Therefore 24 = k(3)(4), so k = 2. Hence y = 2(5)(2) = 20.

examples.question: If y varies partially as x and y = 11 when x = 3, with y = 2x + b, find b.
examples.solution: Substitute the values: 11 = 2(3) + b. Therefore b = 5.

topics.name: Inequalities
topics.description: Inequalities compare quantities using symbols such as <, >, ≤ and ≥. This topic covers linear and quadratic inequalities and their representation on the number line.
objectives: Solve linear inequalities in one variable
Represent inequality solutions on a number line
Apply inequalities to mathematical and practical problems
content: Reversing the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Representation of solutions on a number line

lesson.title: Inequalities
lesson.introduction: An inequality shows that two quantities are not necessarily equal. Instead of an equals sign, inequalities use symbols such as <, >, ≤ and ≥ to describe a range of possible values.

sections.title: Inequality Symbols
sections.content: < means less than, > means greater than, ≤ means less than or equal to, and ≥ means greater than or equal to.

sections.title: Linear Inequalities
sections.content: Linear inequalities can be solved using algebraic operations in much the same way as equations. However, when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, the inequality sign must be reversed.

sections.title: Number-Line Representation
sections.content: Solutions can be shown on a number line. An open circle is used when the boundary value is not included, while a closed circle is used when it is included.

sections.title: Compound Inequalities
sections.content: A compound inequality combines two inequalities. For example, 2 < x ≤ 7 describes all values greater than 2 and less than or equal to 7.

sections.title: Quadratic Inequalities
sections.content: Quadratic inequalities involve expressions such as x² − 5x + 6 > 0. Factorization and a sign analysis across the critical values can be used to determine the solution intervals.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Inequalities can describe limits, ranges and conditions in mathematical and real-life problems.

keyPoints: < means less than.
> means greater than.
≤ means less than or equal to.
≥ means greater than or equal to.
Reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Use an open boundary when the endpoint is excluded.
Use a closed boundary when the endpoint is included.

examples.question: Solve 3x + 2 > 11.
examples.solution: Subtract 2 from both sides: 3x > 9. Divide by 3: x > 3.

examples.question: Solve −2x ≥ 8.
examples.solution: Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the inequality sign: x ≤ −4.

examples.question: Solve 2 < x + 1 ≤ 6.
examples.solution: Subtract 1 throughout: 1 < x ≤ 5.

examples.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 > 0.
examples.solution: Factorize: (x − 2)(x − 3) > 0. The expression is positive outside the two roots, so x < 2 or x > 3.

topics.name: Progression
topics.description: Progression deals with ordered sequences of numbers. This topic covers arithmetic and geometric progressions, their terms, sums and applications.
objectives: Find the common difference of an arithmetic progression
Find the common ratio of a geometric progression
Determine the nth term of an AP or GP
Calculate the sum of a given number of terms
Find missing terms in a progression
Apply progression formulas to mathematical problems
content: nth term of an arithmetic progression
Sum of terms of an arithmetic progression
Finding missing terms in an AP
nth term of a geometric progression
Sum of terms of a geometric progression

lesson.title: Progression
lesson.introduction: A progression is an ordered sequence of numbers that follows a particular pattern. Two important types are arithmetic progression and geometric progression.

sections.title: Arithmetic Progression
sections.content: An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant. This constant is called the common difference and is represented by d.

sections.title: nth Term of an AP
sections.content: The nth term of an arithmetic progression is given by Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term, d is the common difference and n is the position of the term.

sections.title: Sum of an AP
sections.content: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression can be calculated using Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]. It can also be calculated using Sₙ = n/2(a + l), where l is the last term.

sections.title: Geometric Progression
sections.content: A geometric progression is a sequence in which each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant. This constant is called the common ratio and is represented by r.

sections.title: nth Term of a GP
sections.content: The nth term of a geometric progression is Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, where a is the first term, r is the common ratio and n is the position of the term.

sections.title: Sum of a GP
sections.content: For a finite geometric progression where r is not equal to 1, the sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). An equivalent form is Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Progressions can be used to solve problems involving patterns, repeated increases or decreases, savings, growth and other situations where quantities follow a regular sequence.

keyPoints: In an AP, consecutive terms have a constant difference.
Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
In a GP, consecutive terms have a constant ratio.
Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), when r ≠ 1.
Always identify the first term, common difference or ratio, and number of terms before applying a formula.

examples.question: Find the 10th term of the AP 3, 7, 11, 15, ...
examples.solution: Here a = 3, d = 4 and n = 10. Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d = 3 + 9(4) = 39. Therefore, the 10th term is 39.

examples.question: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 2, 5, 8, 11, ...
Find the 6th term of the GP 2, 6, 18, 54, ...
examples.solution: Here a = 2, r = 3 and n = 6. Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹ = 2(3⁵) = 486.

examples.question: Find the sum of the first 5 terms of the GP 1, 2, 4, 8, ...

topics.name: Binary Operations
topics.description: Binary operations combine two elements of a set to produce another element according to a defined rule. This topic covers the definition, properties and applications of binary operations.
objectives: Define a binary operation on a set
Determine whether a set is closed under an operation
Test whether a binary operation is commutative
Test whether a binary operation is associative
Find the inverse of an element
Use operation tables to evaluate binary operations
Solve simple equations involving binary operations

lesson.title: Binary Operations
lesson.introduction: A binary operation is a rule that combines two elements of a set to produce an element according to a specified operation. Common operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication and specially defined operations.

sections.title: Definition
sections.content: A binary operation on a set S combines any two elements of S and produces an element according to a defined rule. The operation may be represented by a symbol such as ★ or ⊙.

sections.title: Closure
sections.content: A set is closed under an operation if applying the operation to any two elements of the set always produces another element of the same set.

sections.title: Commutative Property
sections.content: An operation ★ is commutative if a ★ b = b ★ a for all relevant elements a and b.

sections.title: Associative Property
sections.content: An operation ★ is associative if (a ★ b) ★ c = a ★ (b ★ c) for all relevant elements.

sections.title: Identity Element
sections.content: An identity element leaves another element unchanged when the operation is applied. If e is the identity for ★, then a ★ e = e ★ a = a.

sections.title: Inverse Element
sections.content: An inverse is an element that combines with another element to produce the identity. The exact form of the inverse depends on the operation being used.

sections.title: Operation Tables
sections.content: A binary operation can be represented in a table. The row and column labels represent the two elements being combined, while each cell contains the result of the operation.

sections.title: Solving Binary Operation Problems
sections.content: To solve a problem, substitute the given values into the definition of the operation and simplify carefully. When properties are being tested, compare both sides of the required identity.

keyPoints: A binary operation combines two elements according to a rule.
Closure means the result remains within the set.
Commutative means a ★ b = b ★ a.
Associative means (a ★ b) ★ c = a ★ (b ★ c).
An identity element leaves an element unchanged.
An inverse combines with an element to produce the identity.
Operation tables show the result of combining pairs of elements.

examples.question: A binary operation ★ is defined by a ★ b = a + b + 2. Find 3 ★ 5.
examples.solution: Substitute a = 3 and b = 5: 3 ★ 5 = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10.

examples.question: For the operation a ★ b = a + b + 2, find the identity element.
examples.solution: Let the identity be e. Then a ★ e = a. Therefore a + e + 2 = a, so e = −2.

examples.question: Is ordinary addition commutative?
examples.solution: Yes. For any numbers a and b, a + b = b + a. Therefore addition is commutative.

examples.question: Is ordinary subtraction commutative?
examples.solution: No. In general, a − b is not equal to b − a. For example, 5 − 2 = 3 while 2 − 5 = −3.

topics.name: Matrices and Determinants
topics.description: Matrices are rectangular arrangements of numbers used to organize and solve mathematical problems. This topic covers matrix operations, determinants, inverses and applications to simultaneous equations.
objectives: Determine the order of a matrix
Perform addition and subtraction of matrices
Multiply a matrix by a scalar
Find the transpose of a matrix
Calculate the determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix
Find the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
Use matrices to solve simultaneous linear equations
content: Applications of matrices to simultaneous equations

lesson.title: Matrices and Determinants
lesson.introduction: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers or other mathematical objects in rows and columns. Matrices provide a compact way to organize information and solve systems of equations.

sections.title: Matrix Notation
sections.content: A matrix is written inside brackets and is arranged in rows and columns. The order of a matrix is written as m × n, where m is the number of rows and n is the number of columns.

sections.title: Types of Matrices
sections.content: Common types include row matrices, column matrices, square matrices, zero matrices, diagonal matrices, identity matrices and triangular matrices.

sections.title: Equality of Matrices
sections.content: Two matrices are equal when they have the same order and corresponding elements are equal.

sections.title: Matrix Addition and Subtraction
sections.content: Matrices can be added or subtracted when they have the same order. Corresponding elements are added or subtracted.

sections.title: Scalar Multiplication
sections.content: To multiply a matrix by a scalar, multiply every element of the matrix by that scalar.

sections.title: Matrix Multiplication
sections.content: Two matrices can be multiplied when the number of columns in the first matrix equals the number of rows in the second. Each entry in the resulting matrix is obtained by multiplying corresponding row and column elements and adding the products.

sections.title: Transpose
sections.content: The transpose of a matrix is obtained by changing its rows into columns and its columns into rows.

sections.title: Determinant of a 2 × 2 Matrix
sections.content: For a matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc.

sections.title: Inverse of a 2 × 2 Matrix
sections.content: For a 2 × 2 matrix with a non-zero determinant, the inverse is obtained by dividing the matrix [[d, −b], [−c, a]] by the determinant ad − bc.

sections.title: Applications to Simultaneous Equations
sections.content: Matrices can represent simultaneous linear equations. When the coefficient matrix has a non-zero determinant, its inverse can be used to find the unknown variables.

keyPoints: The order of a matrix is rows × columns.
Matrices must have the same order for addition or subtraction.
Matrix multiplication requires compatible dimensions.
The transpose changes rows into columns.
For [[a, b], [c, d]], determinant = ad − bc.
A matrix has an inverse only when its determinant is non-zero.
The identity matrix acts like 1 in matrix multiplication.

examples.question: Find the determinant of [[3, 2], [1, 4]].
Find the transpose of [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]].
examples.solution: Exchange rows and columns. The transpose is [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]].

examples.question: Find the inverse of [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
examples.solution: The determinant is (2 × 1) − (1 × 1) = 1. Therefore the inverse is [[1, −1], [−1, 2]].

topics.name: Euclidean Geometry
topics.description: Euclidean geometry deals with points, lines, angles, triangles, polygons and circles, together with the relationships between their geometric properties.
objectives: Identify and use basic geometric concepts
Calculate unknown angles using geometric properties
Use properties of triangles to solve problems
Distinguish between congruent and similar figures
Apply properties of polygons and quadrilaterals
Apply basic properties and theorems of circles
content: Theorems involving angles, triangles and circles

lesson.title: Euclidean Geometry
lesson.introduction: Euclidean geometry studies shapes, sizes, angles and the relationships between points, lines and figures on a plane. Many JAMB geometry questions can be solved by recognizing a small number of important properties and theorems.

sections.title: Angles
sections.content: Angles are measured in degrees. Angles on a straight line add to 180°, angles around a point add to 360°, and vertically opposite angles are equal.

sections.title: Parallel Lines
sections.content: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal and alternate angles are equal. Co-interior angles add up to 180°.

sections.title: Triangles
sections.content: The interior angles of a triangle add up to 180°. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

sections.title: Congruence
sections.content: Congruent figures have the same shape and size. Triangles can be shown to be congruent using appropriate conditions such as SSS, SAS and ASA.

sections.title: Similarity
sections.content: Similar figures have the same shape but may have different sizes. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.

sections.title: Polygons
sections.content: A polygon is a closed plane figure made from straight line segments. The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°.

sections.title: Quadrilaterals
sections.content: A quadrilateral has four sides and its interior angles add up to 360°. Important examples include rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses and trapeziums.

sections.title: Circles
sections.content: Important circle concepts include radius, diameter, chord, arc, tangent and sector. Circle theorems can be used to determine unknown angles and lengths.

sections.title: Geometric Constructions
sections.content: Basic constructions include constructing perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and particular angles using standard geometric construction methods.

keyPoints: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
Angles around a point sum to 360°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
The angles of a triangle sum to 180°.
The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
The interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°.
The interior-angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°.
Congruent figures have the same shape and size.
Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.

examples.question: Two angles on a straight line are 65° and x. Find x.
examples.solution: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Therefore x = 180° − 65° = 115°.

examples.question: A triangle has angles 50°, 60° and x. Find x.
examples.solution: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°. Therefore x = 180° − 50° − 60° = 70°.

examples.question: Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.
examples.solution: A hexagon has n = 6 sides. Sum = (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°.

examples.question: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. One alternate angle is 72°. Find the other alternate angle.
examples.solution: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal. Therefore the other angle is 72°.

topics.name: Mensuration
topics.description: Mensuration deals with the measurement of lengths, angles, perimeters, areas, surface areas and volumes of common plane and solid figures.
objectives: Calculate the perimeter of common plane figures
Calculate areas of triangles and quadrilaterals
Calculate the circumference and area of circles
Calculate surface areas of common solids
Apply mensuration formulas to practical problems

lesson.title: Mensuration
lesson.introduction: Mensuration is the study of measurement. It allows us to calculate lengths, perimeters, areas, surface areas and volumes of geometric figures.

sections.title: Perimeter
sections.content: The perimeter of a plane figure is the total distance around its boundary. For a rectangle, perimeter = 2(length + width).

sections.title: Area of Plane Figures
sections.content: Area measures the amount of surface enclosed by a plane figure. Common formulas include area of a rectangle = length × width, triangle = 1/2 × base × height, and parallelogram = base × perpendicular height.

sections.title: Circles
sections.content: The circumference of a circle is 2πr and its area is πr², where r is the radius.

sections.title: Sectors and Arcs
sections.content: A sector is a portion of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc. The arc length and sector area depend on the central angle.

sections.title: Surface Area
sections.content: Surface area is the total area of the outer surfaces of a three-dimensional object. The correct formula depends on the solid.

sections.title: Volume
sections.content: Volume measures the amount of space occupied by a solid. For example, the volume of a cylinder is πr²h and the volume of a prism is the area of its cross-section multiplied by its length.

sections.title: Composite Shapes
sections.content: Complex figures can often be divided into simpler shapes. Calculate each part separately and then combine the results appropriately.

keyPoints: Rectangle area = length × width.
Triangle area = 1/2 × base × perpendicular height.
Circle circumference = 2πr.
Circle area = πr².
Cylinder volume = πr²h.
Prism volume = cross-sectional area × length.
Always use consistent units before calculating.
Area is measured in square units.
Volume is measured in cubic units.

examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 7 cm.
examples.solution: Area = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 12 × 7 = 42 cm².

examples.question: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 7 cm, using π = 22/7.
examples.solution: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm.

examples.question: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm.
examples.solution: Volume = πr²h = π × 3² × 10 = 90π cm³.

examples.question: A rectangle is 8 m long and 5 m wide. Find its perimeter.
examples.solution: Perimeter = 2(8 + 5) = 26 m.

topics.name: Loci
topics.description: A locus is the path traced by a point that moves according to a specified condition. This topic covers common loci and how to construct and interpret them.
objectives: Construct the locus of a point satisfying a given condition
Identify the locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point
Identify the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points
Identify the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines
Use loci to solve geometric construction problems
content: Locus of a point at a fixed distance from a fixed point
Locus of points equidistant from two fixed points
Locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines
Locus involving fixed distances from lines
Applications of loci to geometric problems

lesson.title: Loci
lesson.introduction: A locus is the path followed by a moving point when it is subject to a particular condition. Loci are useful for representing geometric conditions and solving construction problems.

sections.title: Fixed Distance from a Point
sections.content: The locus of points that are a fixed distance from a given point is a circle whose centre is the fixed point and whose radius is the given distance.

sections.title: Equidistant from Two Points
sections.content: The locus of points that are equally distant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining those points.

sections.title: Equidistant from Two Intersecting Lines
sections.content: The locus of points that are equally distant from two intersecting straight lines lies along the angle bisectors of the angles formed by the lines.

sections.title: Construction of Loci
sections.content: A locus can be constructed using geometric tools and by identifying the geometric figure that satisfies the given condition.

sections.title: Intersection of Loci
sections.content: When two or more conditions are given, the required points are found where the corresponding loci intersect.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Loci can be used to find possible positions of points, locations satisfying distance conditions and solutions to geometric construction problems.

keyPoints: A locus is a path satisfying a given condition.
Fixed distance from a point gives a circle.
Equidistance from two points gives a perpendicular bisector.
Equidistance from two intersecting lines gives angle bisectors.
Multiple conditions can be solved by finding intersections of loci.
Always translate the stated condition into a geometric relationship.

examples.question: What is the locus of points that are 5 cm from a fixed point O?
examples.solution: Every point must be exactly 5 cm from O. Therefore the locus is a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm.

examples.question: What is the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B?
examples.solution: The locus is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB.

examples.question: Two straight lines intersect at O. What is the locus of points equidistant from both lines?
examples.solution: The locus consists of the two angle bisectors formed by the intersecting lines.

topics.name: Coordinate Geometry
topics.description: Coordinate geometry uses algebra and coordinates to study points, lines and geometric relationships on the Cartesian plane.
objectives: Locate and interpret points on the Cartesian plane
Find the distance between two points
Find the midpoint of a line segment
Calculate the gradient of a straight line
Determine the equation of a straight line
Find the x- and y-intercepts of a line
Apply coordinate geometry to geometric problems

lesson.title: Coordinate Geometry
lesson.introduction: Coordinate geometry connects algebra with geometry by representing points and lines using numbers. The Cartesian plane allows geometric relationships to be calculated using formulas.

sections.title: The Cartesian Plane
sections.content: The Cartesian plane consists of a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis. Their intersection is the origin, represented by (0, 0). Points are written as ordered pairs (x, y).

sections.title: Distance Between Two Points
sections.content: For points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), the distance is found using the Pythagorean relationship: the square root of [(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].

sections.title: Midpoint
sections.content: The midpoint of a line joining (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is found by averaging the x-coordinates and averaging the y-coordinates.

sections.title: Gradient
sections.content: The gradient or slope of a line measures its steepness. For two points, gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), provided x₂ is not equal to x₁.

sections.title: Equation of a Straight Line
sections.content: A straight line can be represented in forms such as y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept, or y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) when a point and gradient are known.

sections.title: Parallel Lines
sections.content: Two non-vertical straight lines are parallel when they have equal gradients.

sections.title: Perpendicular Lines
sections.content: Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is −1.

sections.title: Intercepts
sections.content: The x-intercept is found by setting y = 0, while the y-intercept is found by setting x = 0.

keyPoints: A point is written as (x, y).
The origin is (0, 0).
Distance uses the differences between the x- and y-coordinates.
The midpoint is obtained by averaging corresponding coordinates.
Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
The form y = mx + c has gradient m and y-intercept c.
Parallel lines have equal gradients.
Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1.

examples.question: Find the distance between A(1, 2) and B(4, 6).
Find the midpoint of A(2, 4) and B(8, 10).
Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).
Find the equation of a line with gradient 3 passing through (2, 5).
examples.solution: Using y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y − 5 = 3(x − 2). Therefore y = 3x − 1.

topics.name: Trigonometry
topics.description: Trigonometry studies the relationships between angles and sides of triangles and their applications to geometric and practical problems.
objectives: Define and apply the sine, cosine and tangent ratios
Calculate unknown sides and angles in right-angled triangles
Use trigonometric values of standard angles
Solve problems involving angles of elevation and depression
Find the area of a triangle using trigonometric ratios
content: Area of a triangle using trigonometry

lesson.title: Trigonometry
lesson.introduction: Trigonometry is the study of relationships between angles and sides of triangles. It is especially useful for finding unknown lengths and angles when enough information about a triangle is known.

sections.title: Trigonometric Ratios
sections.content: For a right-angled triangle, sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. These are commonly remembered as SOH, CAH and TOA.

sections.title: Finding Unknown Sides
sections.content: Choose the trigonometric ratio containing the known side and the unknown side, substitute the known angle and calculate the unknown length.

sections.title: Finding Unknown Angles
sections.content: When the three sides or appropriate side ratio is known, inverse trigonometric functions can be used to determine the angle.

sections.title: Special Angles
sections.content: Important standard angles include 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°. Their sine, cosine and tangent values should be known or obtained when required.

sections.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
sections.content: An angle of elevation is measured upward from a horizontal line, while an angle of depression is measured downward from a horizontal line. Draw a clear diagram before solving.

sections.title: Bearings
sections.content: Bearings give directions measured clockwise from North and are written as three-figure angles, such as 045°, 120° or 270°.

sections.title: Sine Rule
sections.content: For a triangle with sides a, b and c opposite angles A, B and C, the sine rule relates each side to the sine of its opposite angle. It is useful when enough opposite side-angle information is available.

sections.title: Cosine Rule
sections.content: The cosine rule relates two sides and their included angle to the third side. It can also be rearranged to find an angle when all three sides are known.

sections.title: Area of a Triangle
sections.content: When two sides and their included angle are known, the area of a triangle is 1/2 ab sin C.

sections.title: Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
sections.content: The fundamental identity connecting sine and cosine is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

sections.title: Simple Trigonometric Equations
sections.content: Simple equations involving sine, cosine or tangent can be solved by finding the relevant angle and considering the required interval.

keyPoints: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse.
cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA helps remember the three basic ratios.
Bearings are measured clockwise from North and written using three figures.
The sine rule is useful when opposite side-angle information is known.
The cosine rule is useful when two sides and the included angle or all three sides are known.
Area of a triangle = 1/2 ab sin C.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

examples.question: In a right-angled triangle, the opposite side to angle θ is 6 cm and the hypotenuse is 10 cm. Find sin θ.
examples.solution: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = 6/10 = 3/5.

examples.question: A right-angled triangle has an angle of 30° and hypotenuse 12 cm. Find the side opposite the 30° angle.
examples.solution: sin 30° = opposite/12. Since sin 30° = 1/2, opposite = 12 × 1/2 = 6 cm.

examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with sides 8 cm and 10 cm enclosing an angle of 30°.
examples.solution: Area = 1/2 ab sin C = 1/2 × 8 × 10 × sin 30° = 20 cm².

examples.question: A bearing is given as 135°. What direction does this represent?
examples.solution: A bearing is measured clockwise from North. 135° points southeast, halfway between East and South.

topics.name: Differentiation
topics.description: Differentiation is the process of finding the rate at which a quantity changes. It is used to find gradients, rates of change, stationary points and other properties of functions.
objectives: Interpret the derivative as a gradient or rate of change
Use the power rule to differentiate polynomial functions
Apply the sum and difference rules
Apply the product and quotient rules where required
Apply the chain rule to composite functions
Find second and higher derivatives of simple functions

lesson.title: Differentiation
lesson.introduction: Differentiation measures how quickly one quantity changes with respect to another. Geometrically, the derivative gives the gradient of a curve at a particular point.

sections.title: Meaning of the Derivative
sections.content: If y is a function of x, the derivative dy/dx describes the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x. It also represents the gradient of the tangent to the curve at a point.

sections.title: Derivative Notation
sections.content: A derivative may be written as dy/dx, f′(x), or Df(x). These notations represent the same idea when applied to the same function.

sections.title: Differentiation from First Principles
sections.content: The derivative can be defined using a limiting process. For a function f(x), the derivative at x is obtained from the limit of [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h as h approaches zero.

sections.title: Power Rule
sections.content: For a power function xⁿ, the derivative is n xⁿ⁻¹. This rule is especially useful for differentiating polynomial expressions.

sections.title: Constants
sections.content: The derivative of a constant is zero because a constant does not change as x changes.

sections.title: Sum and Difference Rules
sections.content: Differentiate each term separately when a function is a sum or difference of simpler functions.

sections.title: Product Rule
sections.content: For functions u and v, the derivative of uv is u(dv/dx) + v(du/dx).

sections.title: Quotient Rule
sections.content: For functions u and v, the derivative of u/v is [v(du/dx) − u(dv/dx)]/v², where v is not zero.

sections.title: Chain Rule
sections.content: The chain rule is used to differentiate composite functions. If y is a function of u and u is a function of x, then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

sections.title: Higher Derivatives
sections.content: Differentiating a derivative gives a second derivative, commonly written as d²y/dx². Further differentiation gives higher derivatives.

keyPoints: The derivative represents an instantaneous rate of change.
The derivative gives the gradient of a tangent to a curve.
The derivative of a constant is zero.
For y = xⁿ, dy/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹.
Differentiate sums and differences term by term.
Use the product rule when differentiating a product of functions.
Use the quotient rule when differentiating a quotient.
Use the chain rule for composite functions.
The second derivative is obtained by differentiating the first derivative.

examples.question: Differentiate y = x⁵.
examples.solution: Using the power rule, dy/dx = 5x⁴.

examples.question: Differentiate y = 3x⁴ − 2x² + 7.
examples.solution: dy/dx = 12x³ − 4x. The derivative of the constant 7 is zero.

examples.question: Find the derivative of y = (2x + 1)³.
examples.solution: Using the chain rule, dy/dx = 3(2x + 1)² × 2 = 6(2x + 1)².

examples.question: Find the second derivative of y = x⁴.
examples.solution: First derivative: dy/dx = 4x³. Second derivative: d²y/dx² = 12x².

topics.name: Application of Differentiation
topics.description: Applications of differentiation use derivatives to study rates of change, gradients, stationary points, increasing and decreasing functions, maxima, minima and optimization problems.
objectives: Find the gradient of a curve at a given point
Determine equations of tangents and normals
Find stationary points of a function
Distinguish between maximum and minimum stationary points
Use the second derivative to classify stationary points
Determine intervals where a function is increasing or decreasing
Apply differentiation to rates of change and motion
content: Tangent and normal to a curve

lesson.title: Application of Differentiation
lesson.introduction: Differentiation is useful beyond simply finding derivatives. The derivative can describe gradients, rates of change and the behaviour of a function. It can also help find maximum and minimum values.

sections.title: Gradient of a Curve
sections.content: The derivative dy/dx gives the gradient of a curve at a particular point. Substitute the x-coordinate of the point into the derivative to find the gradient there.

sections.title: Tangent to a Curve
sections.content: A tangent is a straight line that touches a curve at a specified point. Its gradient at that point is given by the derivative.

sections.title: Normal to a Curve
sections.content: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent. For non-vertical lines, if the tangent has gradient m, the normal has gradient −1/m.

sections.title: Stationary Points
sections.content: A stationary point occurs where the gradient is zero. Therefore, stationary points are found by solving dy/dx = 0.

sections.title: Maximum and Minimum Points
sections.content: A stationary point can be a local maximum or local minimum. The second derivative can be used to classify it: a positive second derivative indicates a local minimum, while a negative second derivative indicates a local maximum.

sections.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
sections.content: Where the first derivative is positive, a function is increasing. Where the first derivative is negative, the function is decreasing.

sections.title: Rates of Change
sections.content: The derivative gives the rate at which one quantity changes with respect to another. In motion problems, derivatives can connect displacement, velocity and acceleration.

sections.title: Optimization
sections.content: Optimization problems involve finding the greatest or smallest possible value of a quantity. A function is formed, differentiated and stationary points are investigated to identify the required optimum.

keyPoints: dy/dx gives the gradient of a curve.
A stationary point occurs when dy/dx = 0.
A positive second derivative at a stationary point indicates a local minimum.
A negative second derivative at a stationary point indicates a local maximum.
A tangent and its normal are perpendicular.
Positive derivative means the function is increasing.
Negative derivative means the function is decreasing.
Differentiation can be used to solve optimization problems.

examples.question: Find the stationary point of y = x² − 4x + 3.
examples.solution: dy/dx = 2x − 4. Set 2x − 4 = 0, giving x = 2. Substituting into the original function gives y = −1. The stationary point is (2, −1).

examples.question: Classify the stationary point of y = x² − 4x + 3.
examples.solution: The second derivative is d²y/dx² = 2, which is positive. Therefore the stationary point is a minimum.

examples.question: Find the gradient of y = x³ + 2x at x = 2.
examples.solution: dy/dx = 3x² + 2. At x = 2, the gradient is 3(4) + 2 = 14.

examples.question: If the tangent to a curve has gradient 4, find the gradient of its normal.
examples.solution: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent. Therefore its gradient is −1/4.

topics.name: Integration
topics.description: Integration is the reverse process of differentiation. It is used to find antiderivatives, evaluate definite integrals and calculate areas under curves.
objectives: Explain integration as the reverse of differentiation
Find indefinite integrals of simple functions
Use the constant of integration correctly
Integrate polynomial and simple algebraic functions
Apply integration to suitable practical problems

lesson.title: Integration
lesson.introduction: Integration can be viewed as the reverse of differentiation. It allows us to recover a function from its derivative and is also used to calculate areas associated with curves.

sections.title: Meaning of Integration
sections.content: If differentiation changes a function into its derivative, integration reverses this process. An integral therefore represents a family of functions whose derivatives are the original function.

sections.title: Indefinite Integration
sections.content: An indefinite integral does not have specified limits. When integrating, include a constant of integration because different functions can have the same derivative.

sections.title: Basic Integration Rule
sections.content: For a power xⁿ, where n is not −1, the integral is xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C. This is the reverse of the power rule for differentiation.

sections.title: Integrating Polynomial Functions
sections.content: Integrate each term separately. Increase the power of x by one and divide by the new power, while integrating constants according to the basic rules.

sections.title: Definite Integration
sections.content: A definite integral has upper and lower limits. Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit and subtract its value at the lower limit.

sections.title: Area Under a Curve
sections.content: A definite integral can be used to calculate the area between a curve and the x-axis over a specified interval when the function is non-negative on that interval.

sections.title: Area Between Curves
sections.content: The area between two curves can be found by integrating the difference between the upper function and the lower function over the required interval.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Integration can be used in problems involving area, displacement from velocity and other quantities obtained by accumulating a rate of change.

keyPoints: Integration is the reverse process of differentiation.
An indefinite integral includes a constant C.
For xⁿ, the integral is xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C when n ≠ −1.
Integrate sums and differences term by term.
A definite integral is evaluated using its upper and lower limits.
Definite integrals can be used to calculate areas.
Area between curves is found by integrating the difference between the curves.

examples.question: Find ∫ x³ dx.
examples.solution: Increase the power from 3 to 4 and divide by 4. Therefore ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + C.

examples.question: Find ∫ (3x² + 4x) dx.
examples.solution: Integrate each term: ∫3x² dx = x³ and ∫4x dx = 2x². Therefore the result is x³ + 2x² + C.

examples.question: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of x dx.
examples.solution: An antiderivative of x is x²/2. Evaluate: (2²/2) − (0²/2) = 2.

examples.question: Find the area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 2.
examples.solution: Area = ∫₀² x² dx = [x³/3]₀² = 8/3 square units.

topics.name: Representation of Data
topics.description: Representation of data involves organizing and displaying information using tables, charts and graphs so that patterns and relationships can be easily understood.
objectives: Distinguish between common types of data
Interpret line graphs and frequency polygons
Extract information and make conclusions from statistical diagrams

lesson.title: Representation of Data
lesson.introduction: Data is information collected for a particular purpose. Statistical diagrams and tables provide ways of organizing and displaying data so that it can be understood and analyzed more easily.

sections.title: Data
sections.content: Data consists of observations or information collected about people, objects or events. Data may be numerical or categorical.

sections.title: Frequency Tables
sections.content: A frequency table shows the values or classes of data together with the number of times each occurs. Tally marks can be used to count observations before recording their frequencies.

sections.title: Bar Charts
sections.content: A bar chart represents categorical or discrete data using separate bars. The height or length of each bar represents the frequency or value.

sections.title: Histograms
sections.content: A histogram represents grouped continuous data using adjoining bars. When class widths are unequal, frequency density is used so that the areas of the bars represent the frequencies.

sections.title: Pie Charts
sections.content: A pie chart represents parts of a whole as sectors of a circle. The angle of a sector is proportional to the frequency it represents.

sections.title: Line Graphs
sections.content: Line graphs display values using points connected by straight lines. They are useful for showing changes or trends, especially over time.

sections.title: Frequency Polygons
sections.content: A frequency polygon is formed by plotting frequencies against class midpoints and joining the points with straight lines.

sections.title: Cumulative Frequency
sections.content: Cumulative frequency is obtained by progressively adding frequencies. A cumulative frequency curve can be used to estimate quantities such as the median and quartiles.

sections.title: Interpreting Data
sections.content: Statistical diagrams should be read carefully. Compare values, identify trends and use the scale and labels provided before drawing conclusions.

keyPoints: Frequency tells how often a value occurs.
Bar charts use separate bars for categories.
Histogram bars touch because they represent continuous intervals.
Pie-chart sector angles are proportional to frequencies.
Frequency polygons use class midpoints.
Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies.
Always check labels and scales when interpreting a graph.

examples.question: A class has 20 students, and 5 students prefer Mathematics. What angle should represent Mathematics on a pie chart?
The frequencies of three categories are 4, 6 and 10. Find the total frequency.
examples.solution: Total frequency = 4 + 6 + 10 = 20.

examples.question: The frequencies of four groups are 3, 5, 7 and 9. Find the cumulative frequencies.
examples.solution: The cumulative frequencies are 3, 8, 15 and 24.

topics.name: Measures of Location
topics.description: Measures of location describe the central or typical position of a data set. The main measures are the mean, median and mode, together with quartiles and percentiles.
objectives: Explain the meaning of measures of location
Calculate the arithmetic mean of a data set
Calculate the mean from a frequency table
Find the median of a data set
Find the median from a frequency distribution
Identify the mode of a data set
Select an appropriate measure of location for a given data set
content: Choosing an appropriate measure of location

lesson.title: Measures of Location
lesson.introduction: Measures of location summarize a data set by identifying values around which the observations are concentrated. The most common measures are the mean, median and mode.

sections.title: Arithmetic Mean
sections.content: The arithmetic mean is found by adding all observations and dividing by the number of observations. For a frequency distribution, multiply each value by its frequency, add the products and divide by the total frequency.

sections.title: Weighted Mean
sections.content: A weighted mean gives different observations different levels of importance. Multiply each value by its weight, add the products and divide by the sum of the weights.

sections.title: Median
sections.content: The median is the middle value when the observations are arranged in ascending or descending order. For an even number of observations, it is the average of the two middle values.

sections.title: Mode
sections.content: The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set. A data set may have more than one mode or may have no mode.

sections.title: Quartiles
sections.content: Quartiles divide ordered data into four parts. The lower quartile, median and upper quartile are commonly denoted by Q1, Q2 and Q3.

sections.title: Percentiles
sections.content: Percentiles divide ordered data into one hundred parts. The kth percentile is a value below which approximately k percent of the observations fall.

sections.title: Choosing a Measure
sections.content: The mean uses every observation and is sensitive to extreme values. The median is less affected by extreme values, while the mode identifies the most frequent value.

keyPoints: Mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations.
For frequency data, mean = Σfx ÷ Σf.
The median is the middle value of ordered data.
The mode is the most frequently occurring value.
Quartiles divide ordered data into four parts.
The median is the second quartile, Q2.
Percentiles divide data into one hundred parts.
The mean can be strongly affected by extreme values.

examples.question: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12.
Find the median of 3, 7, 9, 12 and 15.
examples.solution: There are five ordered observations, so the middle value is the third value. Median = 9.

examples.question: Find the mode of 2, 4, 4, 5, 6, 4 and 7.
examples.solution: The value 4 occurs more often than any other value. Therefore the mode is 4.

examples.question: A value occurs 3 times, another occurs 5 times and a third occurs 2 times. Find the total frequency.
examples.solution: Total frequency = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10.

topics.name: Measures of Dispersion
topics.description: Measures of dispersion describe how widely data values are spread around a central value. Common measures include range, variance, standard deviation and interquartile range.
objectives: Calculate the range of a data set
Calculate dispersion measures from frequency tables
Compare the spread of different data sets
content: Variance and standard deviation from frequency tables

lesson.title: Measures of Dispersion
lesson.introduction: Measures of dispersion describe the spread or variability of observations. Two data sets may have the same average but very different amounts of variation.

sections.title: Range
sections.content: The range is the difference between the largest and smallest observations. Range = maximum value − minimum value.

sections.title: Interquartile Range
sections.content: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50 percent of the data. It is calculated as Q3 − Q1.

sections.title: Quartile Deviation
sections.content: The quartile deviation, also called the semi-interquartile range, is half the interquartile range: (Q3 − Q1)/2.

sections.title: Variance
sections.content: Variance measures the average squared deviation of observations from their mean. For a population, variance can be calculated using the mean of the squared deviations from the mean.

sections.title: Standard Deviation
sections.content: Standard deviation is the positive square root of variance. It measures the typical spread of observations around the mean.

sections.title: Frequency Distributions
sections.content: For frequency data, frequencies are incorporated into the calculations. Useful formulas include variance = Σf(x − mean)²/Σf and equivalent computational forms.

sections.title: Comparing Data Sets
sections.content: A smaller standard deviation generally indicates that observations are more closely clustered around the mean, while a larger standard deviation indicates greater spread.

sections.title: Coefficient of Variation
sections.content: The coefficient of variation compares standard deviation with the mean. It is commonly expressed as (standard deviation ÷ mean) × 100%.

keyPoints: Range = maximum − minimum.
Interquartile range = Q3 − Q1.
Quartile deviation = (Q3 − Q1)/2.
Variance measures squared spread around the mean.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance.
A smaller standard deviation indicates less spread.
Coefficient of variation = (standard deviation ÷ mean) × 100%.

examples.question: Find the range of 4, 7, 9, 12 and 15.
examples.solution: Range = maximum − minimum = 15 − 4 = 11.

examples.question: If Q1 = 8 and Q3 = 20, find the interquartile range.
If the variance of a data set is 25, find its standard deviation.
examples.solution: Standard deviation = √variance = √25 = 5.

examples.question: Two data sets have the same mean. Set A has standard deviation 3 while Set B has standard deviation 8. Which is more spread out?
examples.solution: Set B is more spread out because its standard deviation is larger.

topics.name: Permutation and Combination
topics.description: Permutation and combination provide methods for counting arrangements and selections of objects without listing every possibility individually.
objectives: Apply counting techniques to practical problems

lesson.title: Permutation and Combination
lesson.introduction: Counting techniques help determine the number of possible arrangements or selections without having to list every possibility. Permutations focus on order, while combinations focus on selection without regard to order.

sections.title: Fundamental Counting Principle
sections.content: If one task can be performed in m ways and another independent task can be performed in n ways, the two tasks together can be performed in m × n ways.

sections.title: Factorial
sections.content: For a positive integer n, n! means n × (n − 1) × (n − 2) × ... × 2 × 1. Also, 0! = 1.

sections.title: Permutations
sections.content: A permutation is an arrangement in which order matters. The number of arrangements of n distinct objects taken r at a time is nPr = n!/(n − r)!.

sections.title: Repeated Objects
sections.content: When some objects are identical, the number of distinct arrangements is reduced because swapping identical objects does not create a new arrangement.

sections.title: Circular Permutations
sections.content: For arrangements of n distinct objects around a circle where rotations are considered identical, the number of arrangements is commonly (n − 1)!.

sections.title: Combinations
sections.content: A combination is a selection in which order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r objects from n distinct objects is nCr = n!/[r!(n − r)!].

sections.title: Permutation versus Combination
