sections.content: Use permutations when the order of selected objects matters. Use combinations when only the selection matters and different orders represent the same choice.

keyPoints: Factorial: n! = n × (n − 1) × ... × 1.
Permutation means arrangement where order matters.
nPr = n!/(n − r)!.
Combination means selection where order does not matter.
For circular arrangements of n distinct objects, the common count is (n − 1)!.
Choose permutation when order matters and combination when it does not.

examples.question: Evaluate 5!.
In how many ways can 3 students be selected from 5 students?
examples.solution: Order does not matter, so use combinations. 5C3 = 5!/(3!2!) = 10.

examples.question: In how many ways can 3 different books be arranged from 5 different books?
examples.solution: Order matters, so use permutations. 5P3 = 5!/(5 − 3)! = 5!/2! = 60.

examples.question: In how many ways can 4 different people sit around a circular table?
examples.solution: For circular arrangements, use (n − 1)!. Therefore (4 − 1)! = 3! = 6.

topics.name: Probability
topics.description: Probability measures how likely an event is to occur. This topic covers basic probability, sample spaces, events, complementary events and combinations of events.
objectives: Calculate the probability of simple events
Use the complement of an event
Apply the addition rule of probability
Apply the multiplication rule of probability
Use tree diagrams to solve probability problems

lesson.title: Probability
lesson.introduction: Probability is a measure of how likely an event is to occur. Its value ranges from 0, representing an impossible event, to 1, representing a certain event.

sections.title: Basic Probability
sections.content: For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event E is P(E) = number of favourable outcomes divided by total number of possible outcomes.

sections.title: Sample Space
sections.content: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. An event is a subset of the sample space.

sections.title: Complementary Events
sections.content: The complement of event A consists of outcomes where A does not occur. P(A complement) = 1 − P(A).

sections.title: Mutually Exclusive Events
sections.content: Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur at the same time. For mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

sections.title: Independent Events
sections.content: Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).

sections.title: Addition Rule
sections.content: For general events A and B, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

sections.title: Multiplication Rule
sections.content: The probability that two events both occur can be found using the appropriate multiplication rule. For independent events, multiply their probabilities.

sections.title: Conditional Probability
sections.content: Conditional probability measures the probability of one event occurring given that another event has occurred. It is written as P(A given B) = P(A and B)/P(B), when P(B) is not zero.

sections.title: Tree Diagrams
sections.content: Tree diagrams organize sequential outcomes and their probabilities. Multiply probabilities along branches and add probabilities for appropriate final outcomes.

keyPoints: Probability lies between 0 and 1.
P(impossible event) = 0.
P(certain event) = 1.
P(E) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes for equally likely outcomes.
P(A complement) = 1 − P(A).
For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Conditional probability uses the information that another event has occurred.

examples.question: A fair die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a 4.
examples.solution: There is one favourable outcome and six possible outcomes. Therefore P(4) = 1/6.

examples.question: If P(A) = 0.3, find P(A complement).
examples.solution: P(A complement) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

examples.question: Two independent events have probabilities 1/2 and 1/3. Find the probability that both occur.
If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2, find P(A or B).
